$comment: The PRESCHOOL THEME year, English (Daily Teaching System, Stage D-4, 2026-11-25; plan decision 5). Designed by one US pre-K teacher-designer from the live English pages (every page looked at on contact sheets), read by one US pre-K coach (130 findings, all applied). Placed by scripts/units/year/place-ready-p.en.theme.js; its texts reach the units through scripts/units/notes/en-theme-p.js. Search heads: docs/SEO/daily-system-demand/preschool-themes.en.json.

pacing.note: One theme a week (Winter, Transportation and Spring take two), from the week after Labor Day to late May; a theme unit has no end days and no check (its measure is the observation checklist).

designNotes: THE YEAR: 30 themes, 33 teaching weeks, from Back to School the week after Labor Day to Camping in late May (September 4, October 4, November 3, December 3, January 4, February 4, March 3 with spring break, April 4, May 4). Three themes run two weeks because their pages and routines fill ten days: Winter (snow and cold, then animals of the cold), Transportation (land and water, then the air) and Spring (baby animals with their mothers, then birds, eggs and nests). Every lesson keeps the order literacy, math, science, motor; the science lesson also carries the social-studies, health and feelings points (families, rules, helpers, habits). ORDER: Community Helpers is the second week of October, the week of Fire Prevention Week (October 9). February opens with Post Office, which builds the class mailbox; Friendship and Valentine's Day follows in the second week of February (the week of February 14 in most years; when the 14th falls on a weekend, teach it the week before), then Doctors and Healthy Habits (Dental Health Month) and Weather. Sports was dropped after review (see leftOut). HOLIDAYS: we are a public pre-K and Head Start program with families of many faiths and none, so the year follows the seasons, not religious holidays. Thanksgiving stays (one week): it is a national, non-religious day about being thankful, harvest food and family, and its science page (Family Traditions) sets a Thanksgiving table beside a Lunar New Year red envelope so every family's celebrations belong. Valentine's Day stays as Friendship and Valentine's Day, built on kindness, taking turns and sharing; every child makes a card for every child. Christmas and Easter are not theme weeks: December is Toys, Cooking and Baking, and Space, and spring is the two-week Spring theme of baby animals and birds; no Christmas or Easter page is handed out (that also rules out the winter pencil path ending at a Christmas tree and a sleigh, and the chick maze whose egg is a decorated Easter egg). Halloween has no pictures and is not a week; the Fourth of July falls in summer vacation. A program with a no-holiday policy can rename those two weeks Harvest and Friendship. PAGES: every page was looked at on a contact sheet; easy copies were chosen where they suit. Card pages whose picture shows another thing than its word (the "timer" alarm clock, the "sky" moon, the "venus" planet, the "turnip" beet, the "squid" octopus, the solid-black "sweatshirt") or that print the British "trousers" were swapped for copies without them; every color space card set carries the "venus" picture, so Space literacy now uses the space word-tracing page, a challenge for the 5s. Four pages are also handed out by a K-3 unit, each because every copy of its type already is: plants-k376-2, healthy-habits-k382, habitats-k383, maps-hard-k722-3. WHAT TO KNOW: (1) Many picture themes have no preschool math type except Ordinal Numbers (Find the Place), so it is the math page in 9 weeks; each of those routines builds a real line first, the teacher reads every chip aloud, 3s do first and last, and the 5s go on to fifth. (2) Most picture themes have only Picture Word Cards for literacy, so 24 weeks use them for vocabulary; every literacy routine has a read-aloud of a picture book about the theme, and every word-card week has a day that claps syllables or hears first sounds in its card words. (3) Stretch pages for the 5s say so in their notes: the name page (writing letters), the family draw-and-count page and the tools Same Number? page (writing numbers), the hand-washing steps (writing 1 to 5), the bugs count-and-trace page (6 to 10), counting back from 10, the space word tracing and the hard land-and-water globe. (4) Camping's science page is Day and Night (a bird, a comet, a star, the sun): the routine (night sky, flashlights, the campfire) makes it camping. Space uses another copy of the same page. (5) The Valentine black-and-white pages show hearts, candy, a key and a lock, but also wedding rings; the notes frame them plainly ("grown-ups who love each other sometimes wear rings"). (6) No food is a play material: sensory trays use sand, apple prints are made with sponges, and every tasting checks for allergies first and serves small, soft pieces.

themes.name: Back to School
themes.searchHead: back to school theme preschool activities
themes.why: Our classroom, its things and its rules: where things go, how we line up, how we keep each other safe.

lessons.title: Back to School: Classroom Word Cards
lessons.objective: Children name four things they use at school (student, scissors, cabinet, pen) and match each picture card to the real thing.
lessons.routine: Take a word walk around the room: hold up a real pen, child-safe scissors and a class name tag, stop at the cabinet, and let each child touch the thing while the class says its name. Read aloud a picture book about the first days of school and point to things we have in our room too. Teach the scissors walk: blades closed, pointing down.
week: Word walk around the room: touch and name the cabinet, a pen, the scissors and a classmate, a student.
Scissors walk at circle: blades closed and pointing down; children pass the scissors and say their name.
Classroom Word Cards: children cut on the dotted lines with help and name each picture.
Card hunt: hide the four cards around the room; finders say the word and lay the card by the real thing.
Clap each card word: pen (1), scis-sors (2), cab-i-net (3); each child takes one card home.

note.mistake: Many children call every writing tool a crayon or a marker and every cupboard a closet, so "pen" and "cabinet" get lost; others think "student" is one child's name, not a word for all of them.
note.words: Say, "This is a pen. It writes like a crayon, but it is thin." Ask, "Who is a student here?" and answer together, "We are all students!" Ask, "What do we keep in the cabinet?"
note.watch: The easy card page shows four big cards: a student holding a book, blue scissors, a red cabinet and a pen. Watch who points to the right card when you say a word, and who can say the word when you point.

lessons.check: Names the student, scissors, cabinet and pen on the cards and in the room

lessons.title: Back to School: First and Last in Line
lessons.objective: Children say who is first, next and last in a line and count from the flag to find the place a chip names.
lessons.routine: Line up for real: five children stand at the door, with a paper flag taped to the door frame. The class counts places from the flag: "first, second, third." Change who stands where and ask, "Who is first now? Who is last?" Then line up five school things on the table (a backpack, a chair, a crayon, a book, a pencil) and count their places from a paper flag the same way.
week: Line leader game at the door: count from the flag who is first, second, third and last.
Five school things in a row on the table; children touch each one and say first, next and last.
Who moved? Swap two school things and say which place each one is in now.
Ordinal Numbers page: the teacher reads each chip aloud; children count from the flag and mark.
Lining up to go outside: each child says their place in line before we walk.

note.mistake: Children start counting at the wrong end of the row or count the flag itself as "first"; others confuse "first" with the number one and look for a picture with a 1 on it instead of the picture next to the flag.
note.words: Put a finger on the flag and say, "We start here. The flag is not a picture." Touch each picture: "First, second, third." Ask, "Which one is first in line? Which one is last?"
note.watch: The page has three rows of five school things (a backpack, a ruler, a chair, a desk, books, a crayon, a globe, a pencil) with a flag at the left and two chips under each row, one with a circle and one with an X. Read each chip aloud; young 3s do first and last.

lessons.check: Says who is first and who is last in a line of five, counting from the front

lessons.title: Back to School: Our Class Rules
lessons.objective: Children tell a picture that follows a class rule (walking inside, cleaning up) from one that does not, and say how the rule keeps us safe.
lessons.routine: Act the rules out in the room. Walk the hallway with walking feet; then the teacher shows one quick step and asks if running inside is safe. Tip out a basket of blocks, sing a clean-up song and put every block back together, then talk about what happens when toys stay on the floor. Take photos of children following each rule for a class rule chart.
week: Practice walking feet in the hallway and talk about why we walk inside.
Clean-up song: tip out the blocks basket and put every block back together.
Our Class Rules page: circle the child who walks and the one who cleans up; cross out the others.
Take photos of children walking and cleaning up for the class rule chart.
Read the rule chart at circle; each child shows one rule with their body.

note.mistake: Young children often circle the picture that looks most fun (the boy running past the lockers) instead of the one that follows the rule, and some think a rule only counts while the teacher is watching.
note.words: Ask, "Is this child using walking feet or running feet?" Say, "We walk inside so nobody gets hurt." Ask, "What happens if the blocks stay on the floor?" Praise with, "You cleaned up, so our room is safe."
note.watch: The page shows two pairs of pictures: a boy walking by the lockers and a boy running past them, and a child in a pink shirt walking away from spilled blocks and the same child putting the blocks into a bin. Watch that the circle and the X go on different pictures in each pair.

lessons.check: Walks inside and helps clean up when asked, and says why the rule helps

titles.picture-tracing-k425-9: Trace and Color the Picture: In the Classroom

lessons.title: Back to School: Pencil Paths and Our Classroom
lessons.objective: Children trace straight, zigzag, bumpy and wavy lines to school things, then trace and color a picture of a classroom.
lessons.routine: Make the lines big first: tape a straight line, a zigzag and a wavy line on the floor and walk them heel to toe. At the table, draw the same lines with a finger in a tray of sand, then with a chunky crayon on big paper. Show the "pinch and hold" grip: the crayon rests between the thumb and two fingers, and the line starts at the dot on the left.
week: Walk the tape lines on the floor: straight, zigzag, bumps and waves.
Finger lines in a sand tray, then chunky crayons on big paper, always left to right.
Pencil Path Practice: trace to the stapler, the scissors, the whiteboard and the desk.
Grip practice: pinch clothespins, roll play-dough snakes and hold the crayon three ways.
In the Classroom page: trace the board, clock, globe, chair, books and backpack, then color.

note.mistake: Children lift the crayon at every point of the zigzag and start each new piece anywhere, or trace from the picture back toward the dot; on the classroom picture they color first and hide the dashed lines.
note.words: Say, "Put your crayon on the orange dot. Go all the way to the stapler without lifting." On the zigzag: "Up the hill, down the hill." On the picture: "Trace every dashed line first, then color."
note.watch: The pencil path page has four lines ending at a stapler, scissors, a whiteboard and a desk; the classroom page has dashed lines for a board, a clock, a globe on a cabinet, a chair, books and a backpack. Look at the grip, the start on the dot and staying on the dashes.

lessons.check: Traces a straight line and a zigzag from the dot to the picture without lifting

themes.name: All About Me
themes.searchHead: all about me theme preschool lesson plans
themes.why: Me: my name, what I like, what I can do, and the five senses I use to learn about the world.

lessons.title: All About Me: My Favorite Things and What I Can Do
lessons.objective: Children tell about themselves (name, age, favorite things, things they can do) in a sentence and mark their choices on the pages.
lessons.routine: Each child brings one favorite thing from home, or picks one in class, for an All About Me basket. At circle the child holds it and finishes, "I like it because..." Read aloud a picture book about a child who is proud of what they can do. Then show real things from the pages (a toothbrush, a ball, a paintbrush, a book) and children stand up for each thing they can do.
week: Show and tell: each child holds a favorite thing and says, "I like it because..."
My Favorite Things page: circle a favorite fruit, pet and instrument; the teacher writes the words.
I can game: stand up if you can run, swim, sing, paint, ride a bike or kick a ball.
I Can page: the teacher reads each sentence; children check the things they can do.
All About Me page: draw yourself, your family and your favorites; the teacher writes name and age.

note.mistake: Children circle every picture in a row because they like them all, or copy a friend's choice; others check "I can swim" because they want to, not because they can, and feel hurt if they are corrected in front of friends.
note.words: Say, "Pick just one. Which fruit do you like the most?" Ask, "Can you do it now, or is it something you want to learn?" Say, "That goes on the 'I want to learn' line. Learning is great!" Model, "My name is ___ and I like ___."
note.watch: The favorite-things page has three rows of six pictures (fruits, pets, instruments) and a line to copy a word; the I Can page shows eight things with boxes and an "I want to learn to" line; the All About Me page has name, age, a self-portrait, a box for the family and three boxes to draw a favorite hobby, treat and vehicle. Read "hobby" as "something you like to do." The teacher writes for the 3s.

lessons.check: Says own name, age and two favorite things in a sentence

lessons.title: All About Me: Count the Letters in My Name
lessons.objective: Children count the letters in their name, one letter per box, and compare with a friend's name to see whose has more.
lessons.routine: Give each child a name strip and a cup of magnetic letters or letter tiles (an adult sits at the table: the pieces are small). Children build their name by matching the strip, then count the letters, touching each one. Lay two names side by side, letter under letter, and see which name has letters left over: that name has more.
week: Find your name card at arrival; at circle, point to each letter of a friend's name as we count.
Build your name with letter tiles (an adult at the table) and count the letters, touching each.
Name partners: lay two names letter under letter and find the one with letters left over.
My Name page: the teacher writes the name; children trace one letter per box and count them.
Name graph: stick name strips in rows by how many letters and count each row.

note.mistake: Children count by saying the letter names or their whole name, or skip a letter and start over in the middle; when they compare, many say the name written bigger or wider has more letters.
note.words: Say, "Touch each letter and count: one, two, three, four." Ask, "How many letters are in your name?" Then, "Let's put our names letter under letter. Whose name has letters left over? That name has more."
note.watch: The page asks for the name one letter per box, how many letters, the first letter, a friend's name, and who has more letters (two bubbles: me, my friend). Writing is a challenge for the 5s; 3s trace what the teacher writes. Watch one touch per letter.

lessons.check: Counts the letters in own name and says whose name has more

titles.five-senses-easy-k355-8: Five Senses: Flower, Sand, Saxophone, Lemon
titles.five-senses-easy-k355-10: Five Senses: Drum, Rock, Lemon, Flower

lessons.title: All About Me: My Five Senses
lessons.objective: Children explore real things and match each one to the body part they use to sense it (hand, ear, tongue, nose).
lessons.routine: Set up sense stations with the real things from the pages: a flower to smell, a drum to hear, a rock and a tray of sand to touch, and lemon slices to smell and, after you check for allergies first, to taste. At each station the child points to the body part they use. Add a feely bag for touch, with only large, safe objects chosen by the teacher.
week: Sense walk: point to eyes, ears, nose, tongue and hands; sing "Head, Shoulders, Knees and Toes."
Sense stations: smell a flower, touch sand and a rock, listen to a drum, smell a lemon.
Five Senses page: draw lines from the flower, sand, saxophone and lemon to the body parts.
Taste and touch (check for allergies first): a lemon slice to taste; guess things in the feely bag.
Second Five Senses page: the drum, rock, lemon and flower; say which sense each one uses.

note.mistake: Children draw every line to the hand because they touch everything, or to the eye because they see it. The lemon has two right answers: you can smell it (nose) or taste it (tongue). Accept both; only the one-line-to-each-part rule makes it the tongue.
note.words: Ask, "Which part of you tells you the drum is loud?" Say, "We hear with our ears." For the lemon: "You can smell it and you can taste it. Both are right!" Ask, "What else could tell you about the sand?"
note.watch: The first page matches a flower, sand, a saxophone and a lemon to a hand, an ear, a tongue and a nose; the second a drum, a rock, a lemon and a flower to the same four. Accept a lemon line to the nose or the tongue and ask the child to say why.

lessons.check: Names which body part hears, smells, tastes and touches

lessons.title: All About Me: Shapes Around My Body
lessons.objective: Children trace rows of circles, squares, triangles and diamonds, starting at the orange dot and following the arrow.
lessons.routine: Make shapes with our bodies: hold hands in a big class circle, stand inside a square of tape on the floor, and make a triangle with three friends' arms. Then trace a circle on a partner's back with a finger and let them guess the shape. Finish with play-dough snakes bent into a circle and a square, and count the corners.
week: Body shapes: a class circle, a tape square on the floor and triangles made with three friends' arms.
Back tracing: draw a circle or a square on a partner's back; the partner guesses the shape.
Circles, Squares and More Shapes: trace the circle row and the square row from the orange dot.
Play-dough snakes bent into circles, squares and triangles; count the corners of each.
Finish the triangle and diamond rows, then find the leg, foot, face and arm pictures.

note.mistake: Children trace a circle in pieces, stopping and starting again, or go the other way round from the arrow; on squares and triangles they round off the corners instead of stopping and turning.
note.words: Say, "Start at the orange dot and go round like the arrow, all the way back home." On a square: "Stop at the corner. Turn. Keep going." Ask, "How many corners did you make?"
note.watch: The page has four rows of dashed shapes (circles, squares, triangles and diamonds), each row with an orange starting dot and an arrow, and a small body picture at the end: a leg, a foot, a face and an arm. Watch for one smooth circle and sharp square corners.

lessons.check: Traces a circle in one stroke and a square with four corners

themes.name: Feelings
themes.why: Naming happy, sad, angry, scared and excited, reading them on faces, and what helps when a feeling is big.

titles.picture-word-cards-easy-emotions-k324-40: Feelings Word Cards: Four Big Faces

lessons.title: Feelings Word Cards: Angry, Tired, Excited and More
lessons.objective: Children name feelings from faces (angry, tired, excited, scared, sad, surprised, shy) and pick the face card that matches how someone looks.
lessons.routine: Pass a hand mirror around the circle: the teacher names a feeling and each child makes that face, then shows a partner. Read aloud a picture book about big feelings and stop to ask how the character feels. Act out short moments with a puppet (its block tower falls, it gets a hug, a loud noise surprises it); children hold up the face card that matches.
week: Mirror faces: make happy, sad, angry and surprised faces and look at them in the mirror.
Feelings Word Cards (four faces): angry, tired, content and excited; the teacher cuts the cards.
Puppet moments: the puppet's tower falls; children hold up the card for how it feels.
Feelings Word Cards (eight faces): add shy, merry, scared, sad and surprised.
Feelings charades: a friend finds the card, then we clap it: sad (1), an-gry (2), ex-cit-ed (3).

note.mistake: Children call every unhappy face "sad" and every smiling face "happy," so tired, angry and scared all become sad. The words "content" and "merry" are new to most: give them kid meanings first (calm and happy, very jolly).
note.words: Say, "Look at the eyebrows. They are pulled down. This face is angry." Ask, "Is this face sad or tired? Look at the eyes." Say, "Content means calm and happy, like after a hug. Merry means happy and laughing."
note.watch: The first card page shows four big faces (angry, tired, content and excited); the second has eight smaller faces (shy, merry, content, tired, scared, sad, excited and surprised). Listen for feeling words other than happy and sad.

lessons.check: Names at least four feelings from faces: happy, sad, angry and scared

lessons.title: Feelings Faces in a Row: First, Next, Last
lessons.objective: Children say first, next and last for a row of faces and count from the flag to find a face's place.
lessons.routine: Five children stand in a row at the front holding face cards, with a paper flag taped at one end. Ask, "Who is first? Who is last?" and count places together from the flag. Then a child calls out a feeling; the child holding that face steps forward and says, "I am third." Mix up the line and play again so every child gets a turn.
week: Feelings line: five children hold face cards; count first, second and third from the flag.
Who moved? Two faces swap places; the class says the new first and last.
Call a feeling: the child with that face says their place, "I am fourth."
Ordinal Numbers page: the teacher reads each chip; children count faces from the flag and mark.
Lining up: each child says their place in line and one feeling they have today.

note.mistake: Children look for the face that "matches" the number word instead of counting places, or start from the right side because their favorite face is there. Many 3s know first and last but guess the places in between.
note.words: Say, "Start at the flag. Count each face: first, second, third." Ask, "Which face is last in this row?" Read a chip: "This one says third, with an X. Find the third face and make an X."
note.watch: The page shows three rows of five round faces (puzzled, crying, laughing, worried, angry, surprised and more) with a flag at the left and two chips under each row, each chip with a circle or an X. Read every chip aloud; 3s may do first and last only.

lessons.check: Finds the first, third and last face in a row of five

lessons.title: Feelings: How Would You Feel?
lessons.objective: Children say how they would feel in everyday moments and sort faces into feelings that feel good and feelings that feel bad.
lessons.routine: Make a feelings corner with a soft pillow and a plastic calm-down bottle (glitter and water inside, lid glued shut). Show things that bring feelings: a party hat, a toy spider, a picture of an ice cream cone, a cozy blanket. For each, children make a face and say, "I would feel..." Teach one calm-down tool: smell the flower, blow out the candle.
week: Feelings corner tour: the calm-down bottle and "smell the flower, blow out the candle."
How would you feel? A party hat, a toy spider and a cozy blanket: make the face and say it.
How Do You Feel? page: circle a face for rain, a spider, a party, ice cream, bedtime and a sleeping bag.
Feels good or feels bad: sort feeling face cards into two baskets and say why.
Feels Good or Feels Bad page: draw a line from each face to its box; share a calm-down tool.

note.mistake: Children think there is one right face for each picture and get upset when a friend fears the spider they like. On the sort page, many read the first face (eyes squeezed shut, mouth wide open) as laughing and put it under feels good: look at the eyebrows. Any face is right if the child can say why.
note.words: Ask, "How would you feel if rain came on your picnic?" Say, "Some friends feel scared of spiders, and some feel happy. Both are okay." Ask, "Does angry feel good or bad inside your body?" Say, "When I feel bad, I can smell the flower and blow out the candle."
note.watch: The first page has six pictures (a rain cloud, a spider, a party hat with a cake, an ice cream cone, slippers and the moon, a sleeping bag), each with two faces to choose from; the second has four faces to sort into Feels good and Feels bad. Accept any face the child explains.

lessons.check: Names how they feel and uses one calm-down tool when a feeling is big

lessons.title: Feelings Faces Pencil Paths: Lines and Crosses
lessons.objective: Children trace straight, zigzag, bumpy and wavy paths and draw down lines, slants and crosses toward feeling faces.
lessons.routine: Move the lines to music: march in a straight line to a happy song, jump a zigzag, and sway like waves to a calm song. Then paint with water on the fence or a chalkboard outside: tall down lines, slanted lines and crosses. Children show the face that matches the music: a happy march, a sleepy wave.
week: Feelings music: march straight lines to happy music, sway in waves to calm music.
Pencil Path Practice: trace each line to its feeling face and name the face at the end.
Water painting on the fence or chalkboard: tall down lines, slants and crosses.
Down Lines, Slants and Crosses: start at the top dot and pull each line down.
Draw a happy face and a sad face with lines and curves; tell a friend which is which.

note.mistake: Children push the crayon up from the bottom on down lines, so the lines wobble, and draw crosses as two lines that miss each other; on the slants they turn the paper instead of moving their hand.
note.words: Say, "Start at the top dot and pull down, like rain falling." For a cross: "Down, then across, and make them meet in the middle." Ask, "What face is waiting at the end of this line?"
note.watch: The pencil path page has a straight line, a zigzag, bumps and waves, each ending at a feeling face; the second page has rows of down lines, crosses, slants both ways and X crosses, also ending at faces. Check top-to-bottom strokes and lines that meet.

lessons.check: Draws a down line from top to bottom and a cross whose lines meet

themes.name: My Family and My Home
themes.why: Who is in my family, that families come in many kinds, and the rooms and things of the home we share.

titles.picture-word-cards-easy-around-the-house: Home Word Cards: Stairs, Desk, Dustpan, Fan
titles.picture-word-cards-easy-home-bw-2-k324-5: Home Word Cards to Color: Toaster, Blender, Iron

lessons.title: My Family and My Home: Home Word Cards
lessons.objective: Children name things in a home (stairs, desk, dustpan, fan, toaster, blender, armchair, iron) and tell which room each belongs in.
lessons.routine: Turn the house corner into a home with a real dustpan and brush, a small desk and toy kitchen things. Children play family while the teacher narrates with the words: "Grandma sweeps with the dustpan." Read aloud a picture book about a family at home and name each room. Ask families to send a photo of one room at home.
week: House corner opens: play family with a real dustpan, a desk and toy kitchen things.
Home Word Cards: stairs, desk, dustpan, fan; desk and dustpan start the same: /d/, /d/!
Which room? Put each card in a kitchen, bedroom or living room box and say why.
Home Word Cards to color: the toaster, blender, armchair and iron; color and name them.
Family photo share: point to the room in your photo and name one thing in it.

note.mistake: The stairs card looks like stacked colored blocks, so many children say "blocks"; "steps" is a fine word too. Children call the dustpan a "shovel," and every kitchen machine a "mixer." Some say a thing belongs where it is in their own home (the iron "lives in the closet"), which is true for them.
note.words: Say, "This is a dustpan. We sweep the crumbs into it." Ask, "Where is the toaster in your home? In the kitchen?" Say, "In some homes the iron stays in a closet. Where is it at your house?"
note.watch: The color cards show stairs, a desk with a lamp, a dustpan and a fan; the black-and-white cards show a toaster, a blender, an armchair and an iron to color. Listen for the right word and for where each one is used at home.

lessons.check: Names four home things and says which room each one belongs in

lessons.title: My Family: Draw and Count Who Lives With Me
lessons.objective: Children draw their family and count the people and pets, showing each number on a ten-frame.
lessons.routine: Each child brings a family photo or draws one at the easel. On a big ten-frame on the rug, the child puts one large counter for each person in the family, then one for each pet, and the class counts together, touching each counter. Families are different: count whoever the child says lives with them or takes care of them.
week: Family photos on the board: each child counts the people in their own photo.
Big ten-frame on the rug: one counter for each family member; count together.
All About My Family page: draw your family in the big box.
Fill the page's ten-frames for people, brothers, sisters and pets; the teacher helps write.
Family line-up: children stand behind the number card for the people in their family.

note.mistake: Children count themselves twice or forget to count themselves; others count everyone they love (cousins, a grandma far away) and get a very big number. Accept the child's family and help them choose who lives with them for the boxes.
note.words: Ask, "Who lives at your house? Let's put one counter for each person." Say, "Don't forget you! You count too." Ask, "No pets? Then that ten-frame stays empty."
note.watch: The page has a big box to draw the family, then four parts (people in my family, brothers, sisters and pets), each with a ten-frame to color and a box for the number. Writing the number is for the 5s; younger children fill the frame and say it.

lessons.check: Counts the people in their family drawing, touching each one once

titles.family-easy-k714-3: Many Kinds of Families: First Set of Families
titles.family-easy-k714-4: Many Kinds of Families: Second Set of Families

lessons.title: My Family: Many Kinds of Families
lessons.objective: Children see that families come in many kinds and draw a person who takes care of them.
lessons.routine: Build a family board from photos families send in, or drawings made at school. Look at them at circle: big families and small ones, families with grandparents, two moms, one dad, foster families. Put family figures in the block area to build their homes. Each child tells who takes care of them and one thing that person does.
week: Family board: look at the photos and say who is in each family.
Block homes: build a home for a family of figures and tell who lives there.
Many Kinds of Families page: look at the three families and draw someone who cares for you.
Helping at home: who cooks, who reads at bedtime, who brings you to school?
Second Many Kinds of Families page: draw another person who cares for you and say their name.

note.mistake: Children say a family "has to have" a mom and a dad, or that a family with only a grandma is "not a real family." Some draw a pet or a friend as the one who cares for them. Accept every family the child names.
note.words: Say, "Every one of these is a family." Ask, "Who takes care of you? What does that person do for you?" Say, "Families can be big or small. They are all families."
note.watch: Both pages show three family pictures of different sizes and kinds, a big box to draw someone who cares for me, and a line where the teacher writes the names the child says. Listen for "every one is a family."

lessons.check: Says that families are different and names a person who cares for them

titles.picture-tracing-k418: Picture Tracing: The Path to the Door

lessons.title: My Home: Trace the House and the Path to the Door
lessons.objective: Children trace a home and garden picture, a house made of shapes and pencil paths to home things, starting at the dot.
lessons.routine: Draw a chalk path from the playground gate to the classroom door; children walk it, then push toy cars along it. Inside, build a house from big cardboard blocks and glue a paper house: a square, a triangle roof and a small square window. Children tell what is inside their own home.
week: Chalk path outside from the gate to the door: walk it, then drive toy cars on it.
Paper shape house: glue a square, a triangle roof and a square window.
The Path to the Door page: trace the house, the path, the tree, the sun and the rabbit.
The Shape House page: trace the square, triangle and circles, then color every circle.
Pencil Path Practice: trace lines to the grill, the pan, the iron and the cushion.

note.mistake: On the big garden picture children trace only the house and skip the small parts (flowers, butterfly, rabbit); on the shape house they color the circles before tracing them and color the roof too.
note.words: Say, "Follow the path all the way to the door." Ask, "What shape is the roof? A triangle." Say, "Trace every shape first. Then color only the circles."
note.watch: The garden page shows a house with a path, a tree, a sun, a cloud, a butterfly, tulips and a rabbit, all dashed; the shape house page has a square house, a triangle roof, a square window, and a triangle and two circles beside it; the pencil paths end at a grill, a pan, an iron and a cushion.

lessons.check: Traces a whole house picture along the dashes and names its shapes

themes.name: Apples and Fruits
themes.why: Apples and other fruits at harvest time: eating an apple from first bite to core, big and small apples, fruit or vegetable.

lessons.title: Apples and Fruits: First, Next, Last With an Apple
lessons.objective: Children put three pictures of an apple being eaten in order and tell the story with first, next and last.
lessons.routine: Check for allergies first. Show a whole apple, take one bite, and keep eating until only the core is left, taking a photo at each step (the children eat thin apple slices the teacher cuts). Children retell with the photos: "First the apple is whole, next it has a bite, last it is a core." Read aloud a picture book about apples and retell it with first, next and last.
week: Real apple story (check for allergies first): whole apple, one bite, a core; take a photo of each.
Retell with the three photos: first, next, last; mix them up and fix the order.
Story Sequencing page: cut the three apple pictures and glue them under First, Next, Last.
Play-dough apple: make it whole, take a "bite," make a core, and tell each step.
Tell the apple story to a friend with the glued page, using first, next and last.

note.mistake: Children glue the pictures in the order they cut them out, or put the core first because it is the smallest; some think the bitten apple and the core are two different apples.
note.words: Ask, "What happened first? The apple was all whole." Say, "Next, someone took a bite. Last, only the core is left." Ask, "Can the core come first? Why not?"
note.watch: The page shows three empty frames on a line (First, Next and Last) and a strip at the bottom with a whole apple, an apple with a bite and an apple core, each on a plate. Cutting the strip is part of the work; help 3s with the scissors.

lessons.check: Puts three apple pictures in order and tells it with first, next and last

lessons.title: Apples and Fruits: Find the Big Apples
lessons.objective: Children compare apples by size and circle every big one.
lessons.routine: Bring real apples of very different sizes. Children sort them into a big basket and a small basket, holding two at once to feel the difference, then line them up and find the biggest. At snack, after checking for allergies, the teacher slices one big apple and one small apple and the class counts how many slices each one makes.
week: Apple sort: real big and small apples go into a big basket and a small basket.
Hold two apples: which is bigger? Line up the apples from small to big together.
Big Ones Only page: circle every big apple and leave the small ones alone.
Big and small hunt: a big block and a small block, a big book and a small book.
Snack (check for allergies first): count the thin slices from a big apple and a small apple.

note.mistake: Children circle the apples they like, or every apple, or one big apple and then stop because they think there is only one answer. Small apples that sit next to big ones get circled by mistake.
note.words: Ask, "Is this apple big or small?" Say, "Put your two hands around it. Big!" Ask, "Are there more big apples? Keep looking." Say, "Leave the small ones alone."
note.watch: The page shows red apples scattered over the page, some big and some small, with no words to read; the child circles every big one. Count the big apples yourself first so you know how many circles to look for.

lessons.check: Circles every big apple and leaves the small ones

titles.science-sort-easy-k202-3: Fruits and Vegetables: Orange, Strawberry, Lettuce
titles.science-sort-easy-k202-4: Fruits and Vegetables: Orange, Apple, Carrot

lessons.title: Apples and Fruits: Is It a Fruit or a Vegetable?
lessons.objective: Children sort real foods and pictures into fruits and vegetables, using seeds as a clue.
lessons.routine: Check for allergies first. Bring an orange, an apple, a strawberry, a carrot, broccoli and lettuce. The teacher cuts the apple and the orange open and the class finds the seeds: a fruit carries seeds. Look at the carrot (a root) and the broccoli (the flower part). Children sort the real foods onto two placemats, Fruits and Vegetables, then taste small pieces: thin apple slices, orange sections, and carrot and broccoli steamed soft.
week: Fruit and vegetable basket (check for allergies first): touch, smell and name each one.
Find the seeds: the teacher cuts an apple and an orange; seeds mean it is a fruit.
Fruits and Vegetables page: lines from the orange, strawberry, broccoli and lettuce to the boxes.
Sort the real foods onto two placemats; taste small soft pieces (carrot and broccoli steamed, not raw).
Second Fruits and Vegetables page: the orange, apple, carrot and broccoli.

note.mistake: Children sort by color (red with red) or call everything sweet a fruit and everything green a vegetable; the strawberry's seeds are on the outside, so many say it has none.
note.words: Ask, "Does it have seeds inside? Let's look." Say, "A strawberry wears its seeds on the outside." Ask, "Where does a carrot grow? Under the ground. It is a root, a vegetable."
note.watch: The first page shows an orange, a strawberry, broccoli and lettuce above a Fruits box and a Vegetables box; the second an orange, an apple, a carrot and broccoli. The child draws a line from each dot to a box. Watch who sorts by color instead of seeds.

lessons.check: Sorts an apple, an orange, a carrot and broccoli into fruits and vegetables

lessons.title: Apples and Fruits: Trace Big, Middle and Small Fruit
lessons.objective: Children trace apples and bananas from big to small and follow pencil paths to fruit.
lessons.routine: Make apple prints with apple-shaped sponges, a big one and a small one, dipped in red paint. Roll play-dough into a big, a middle and a small apple and line them up. Run a finger along the curve of a real banana before tracing the paper ones.
week: Apple prints: stamp big and small apple-shaped sponges in red paint.
Play-dough fruit: roll a big, a middle and a small apple and a curved banana.
Big, Medium, Small page: trace the apples, then the bananas, always the big one first.
Finger-trace the curve of a real banana, then draw the curve in the air.
Pencil Path Practice: trace each line to its fruit and name it: persimmon, apple, orange, peach.

note.mistake: Children trace the small apple first because it is quick, or trace the bananas in many short pieces; on the pencil paths they stop at each corner of the zigzag and go back over the line.
note.words: Say, "Trace the big apple first, then the middle one, then the small one." Ask, "Which apple is the biggest?" On the banana: "One long curve, like a smile lying on its side."
note.watch: The first page, titled Big, Medium, Small, has a row of three dashed apples and a row of three dashed bananas from big to small; the pencil path page has a straight line, a zigzag, bumps and waves ending at a persimmon, an apple, an orange and a peach. Watch the order big, middle, small.

lessons.check: Traces three apples in order from big to small

themes.name: Community Helpers
themes.searchHead: community helpers preschool theme lesson plan
themes.why: The people who help us (firefighters in Fire Prevention Week, gardeners, doctors, cashiers) and the tools they use.

titles.picture-word-cards-easy-occupations-k324: Helper Word Cards: Teacher, Musician, Gardener

lessons.title: Community Helpers Word Cards: People Who Help Us
lessons.objective: Children name community helpers (teacher, gardener, cashier, doctor, veterinarian and more) and tell what each one does.
lessons.routine: Invite one helper to visit (the school nurse, a cafeteria cook, or a firefighter in Fire Prevention Week) and let each child ask one question. Read aloud a picture book about people who help in a town. Open a dress-up box with hats and toy tools; a child dresses as a helper and the class guesses who it is and what that helper does.
week: Helper visit: a school helper or a firefighter answers the children's questions.
Helper Word Cards: teacher, musician, gardener and cashier; say what each one does.
Dress-up guessing game: a child dresses as a helper and friends guess who it is.
Helper Word Cards (eight): add the new jobs and clap them: tai-lor (2), phar-ma-cist (3).
Thank-you pictures: each child draws a helper and tells how that helper helps us.

note.mistake: Children name helpers by their tool ("the hammer man") or call everyone in a uniform "police." The words pharmacist, veterinarian and tailor are new: name each picture first and give a simple meaning.
note.words: Say, "A veterinarian is an animal doctor." Ask, "Who sells us food at the store? A cashier." Say, "A tailor sews and fixes clothes." Say, "Every job helps someone. A singer and a musician help us feel happy." Ask, "Who helps us here at school?"
note.watch: The first page shows four big cards (a teacher, a musician, a gardener and a cashier); the second has eight smaller cards (athlete, pharmacist, gardener, doctor, cashier, tailor, veterinarian and singer). Watch whether the child adds what the helper does.

lessons.check: Names four community helpers and says what each one does

lessons.title: Community Helpers: Dot-to-Dot Garbage Truck
lessons.objective: Children count from 1 to 10 in order and join the dots to finish the garbage truck.
lessons.routine: Watch for the garbage truck on pickup day (or look at a photo) and talk about the sanitation workers who keep our streets clean. Line up ten paper-cup trash cans numbered 1 to 10; children drive a toy truck to each can in order and pick it up, counting aloud. Mix up two cups and let the class fix the order.
week: Who cleans our street? Watch for the garbage truck or look at a photo of the workers.
Toy truck pickup: drive to paper-cup cans numbered 1 to 10, in order, counting aloud.
Fix the order: two cups swap places; children put them back in counting order.
Dot-to-Dot 1 to 10: join the dots to finish the front of the garbage truck.
Clean-up count: pick up ten blocks and drop each in the bin, counting aloud.

note.mistake: Children draw to the closest dot instead of the next number, and many lose their place after 5 and start again at 1; some draw lines across the truck picture instead of from dot to dot.
note.words: Say, "Find 1. Now say the next number: 2." Ask, "Where is 6? Look carefully." Say, "When we join 9 to 10, the truck is finished."
note.watch: The page shows a garbage truck with its back, wheels and cab windows drawn; dots 1 to 10 run from 1 by the front bumper up the front of the cab and across its roof to 10, with a number strip from 1 to 10 at the bottom to help the child find the next number.

lessons.check: Joins dots 1 to 10 in order, saying each number

titles.science-match-easy-k213-3: Helpers and Tools: Teacher, Doctor, Builder, Gardener
titles.science-match-easy-k213-6: Helpers and Tools: Firefighter, Teacher, Doctor, Builder

lessons.title: Community Helpers and Their Tools
lessons.objective: Children match helpers (a teacher, a doctor, a builder, a gardener, a firefighter) to the tools they use.
lessons.routine: Set up a tool table with safe real or toy tools: a toy stethoscope and thermometer, a book, a toy hammer, a garden rake (for outside), a toy ladder and a firefighter hat. A child picks a tool and acts out how it is used, and the class names the helper. Visit the nurse's office or the school garden to see real tools at work.
week: Tool table: pick a toy tool, act out how it is used, and the class names the helper.
Visit the nurse's office or the school garden to see real tools at work.
Helpers and Tools page: the teacher, doctor, builder and gardener and their tools.
Helper relay: carry a toy tool to the helper picture it goes with.
Second tools page: the firefighter, teacher, doctor and builder; find the tool nobody needs.

note.mistake: Children match by color (the red hammer with the red firefighter) or give the ladder to the builder, which can also be right. Both pages have five tools for four helpers, so one is left over, but children think every tool must get a line.
note.words: Ask, "Who uses a ladder to reach a fire?" Say, "Some tools are used by more than one helper." Say, "One tool is left over. That's okay."
note.watch: The first page has a teacher, a doctor, a builder and a gardener beside a hammer, a ladder, a rake, a needle and a book; the second a firefighter, a teacher, a doctor and a builder beside a thermometer, a ladder, a tractor, a hammer and a book. Accept a sensible match the child explains.

lessons.check: Matches four helpers to their tools and says what each tool does

titles.maze-puzzles-easy-k405-8: Picture Maze: Help the Firefighter Reach the Fire Truck

lessons.title: Community Helpers Maze: The Firefighter and the Truck
lessons.objective: Children follow a winding road with a crayon to help the firefighter reach the fire truck.
lessons.routine: Practice the fire drill route: walk the exit path from the classroom to the meeting spot outside, then talk about firefighters who come in their truck. Lay a blue tape road on the floor that bends and splits, and children walk the firefighter's way to a toy fire truck. Practice "stop, drop and roll" on the rug.
week: Fire drill walk: follow our exit path to the meeting spot outside.
Stop, drop and roll on the rug; look at pictures of a firefighter's coat and helmet.
Tape road on the floor: walk the firefighter's way to the toy fire truck.
Picture Maze: draw a line along the road from the firefighter to the fire truck.
Draw your own road for a toy car on big paper and drive along it.

note.mistake: Children cut across the grass to the truck because it is close in a straight line, or stop where two roads meet and take the one that points at the truck, then reach a dead end and give up.
note.words: Say, "Firefighters stay on the road. Keep your crayon between the edges." Ask, "Where do the roads split? Which way goes to the truck?" Say, "Dead end? Go back to the split and try again."
note.watch: The maze shows a wide gray road winding through the grass, with town buildings in the background, the firefighter at the bottom left and the fire truck at the right, and a house, a fence and a bike beside the road. Watch the crayon at each split.

lessons.check: Follows a winding road with a crayon to the goal and goes back at dead ends

themes.name: Farm
themes.searchHead: farm animals theme preschool lesson plans
themes.why: Farm animals and farm work: who lives on the farm, what farm animals eat, and which animals are farm and which are wild.

titles.picture-word-cards-easy-farm-animals-k32: Farm Word Cards: Hen, Cow, Pig, Sheep
titles.picture-word-cards-easy-farm-bw-k324-44: Farm Word Cards to Color: Tractor, Goat, Farmer

lessons.title: Farm Word Cards: Animals and Farm Things
lessons.objective: Children name farm animals and farm things (hen, cow, pig, sheep, goat, tractor, wheelbarrow, farmer) and tell the sound or job of each.
lessons.routine: Sing "Old MacDonald Had a Farm" with toy farm animals, and each child chooses the next animal. Read aloud a picture book about a farm and make each animal's sound when it appears. Build a farm in the block area with a toy barn and tractor, and push a child-size wheelbarrow outside while acting out farm jobs: feeding the hens, driving the tractor.
week: Sing "Old MacDonald Had a Farm" with toy animals; each child picks the next animal.
Farm Word Cards: hen, cow, pig and sheep; say each name and the animal's sound.
Block-area farm: build a barn and pens; put each card where its animal lives.
Color the wheelbarrow, tractor, goat and farmer; clap goat (1), trac-tor (2), wheel-bar-row (3).
Wheelbarrow work outside: push leaves or straw and tell what the farmer does.

note.mistake: Children call the hen "chicken" and the sheep "lamb" (accept both and stretch them), and mix up goat and sheep because both have hooves and fur; most call every farm machine a "truck."
note.words: Say, "This is a hen. A hen is a mother chicken." Ask, "Is it a sheep or a goat? Look for the beard and the horns." Say, "A tractor pulls heavy things. A wheelbarrow carries them."
note.watch: The color cards show a hen, a cow, a pig and a sheep; the black-and-white cards show a wheelbarrow, a tractor, a goat and a farmer to color. Listen for the animal's name plus what it gives or does (eggs, milk, wool).

lessons.check: Names four farm animals and one thing a farmer uses

lessons.title: Farm: Connect the Dots 1 to 10 to Make a Duck
lessons.objective: Children say the numbers 1 to 10 in order and join the dots in that order to finish a duck.
lessons.routine: Count real things in order before the dots: ten toy ducks in a row, one number for each duck the child touches. Lay paper plates numbered 1 to 10 in a path on the floor and children hop from 1 to 10, saying each number. Then play "What comes next?": the teacher says a number on a plate and the class says the next one.
week: Ten toy ducks in a row: touch and count each one from 1 to 10.
Number plate path: hop from 1 to 10 on the floor, saying each number.
What comes next? The teacher says a number; the class says the next one.
Dot-to-Dot 1 to 10: start at 1 by the beak and join the dots over the duck's head and down its back.
Count the farm toys in the block area to 10, then color the finished duck.

note.mistake: Children connect the dots by distance, jumping to the nearest dot instead of the next number; others skip from 6 to 9 because they cannot find 7, or start at the biggest number they know.
note.words: Say, "Put your crayon on 1. Now find 2. Say it, then draw to it." Ask, "What comes after 6?" Say, "Look for the number, not the closest dot."
note.watch: The page shows a duck with its beak, eye, chest, wing and feet drawn; dots 1 to 10 make the top of its head and its back down to the tail, with no lines between them. Watch the child say each number before drawing to it.

lessons.check: Says the numbers 1 to 10 in order and joins the dots in that order

lessons.title: Farm: Farm Animals and Wild Animals
lessons.objective: Children sort animals into farm animals and wild animals and tell who takes care of each.
lessons.routine: Put a toy barn and a box of grass and toy trees (the wild) on the rug. Children pull toy animals from a bag (a horse, a cow, a goat, a pig, an elephant, a zebra, a lion) and decide: does a farmer take care of it, or does it live in the wild? Talk about what farm animals give us (milk, eggs, wool) and why an elephant does not live on a farm.
week: Toy animal bag: pull an animal, say its name and where it lives.
Barn or wild? Sort the toy animals and tell why each one goes there.
Farm and Wild Animals page: lines from the horse, elephant, goat and zebra to the boxes.
What farm animals give us: milk, eggs and wool; feel a ball of wool.
Build a farm and a wild place in the block area and put each toy animal home.

note.mistake: Children sort by size (big animals are wild) or by color, and many call the zebra a striped horse that lives on a farm; some put the goat with the wild animals because it has horns.
note.words: Ask, "Does a farmer take care of this animal?" Say, "A zebra looks like a horse, but it lives in the wild." Ask, "What does a goat give the farmer?"
note.watch: The page shows a horse, an elephant, a goat and a zebra above two boxes, Farm Animals and Wild Animals; the child draws a line from the dot under each animal to a box. Watch the zebra and the horse.

lessons.check: Sorts a horse, a goat, an elephant and a zebra into farm and wild

titles.maze-puzzles-easy-k406-5: My First Maze: Help the Hen Get to the Corn
titles.maze-puzzles-hard-k406-12: My First Maze: Help the Horse Get to the Carrot

lessons.title: Farm Mazes: Hen, Horse, and Babies and Mothers
lessons.objective: Children draw a line along a wide maze road from the start to the goal without crossing the edges.
lessons.routine: Make a farm maze on the floor with masking tape and chairs: wide roads and one dead end. Children push a toy tractor through it, then walk it as a hen looking for corn. In a sand tray, children drag a finger along a road the teacher draws. Talk about dead ends: "Oops, turn around and try another way."
week: Floor maze with tape and chairs: walk from the barn to the corn and find the dead end.
My First Maze: draw a line along the wide road from the hen to the corn.
Sand tray roads: push a toy tractor along a road the teacher draws.
My First Maze: find the road from the horse to the carrot; back up at dead ends.
Babies and Mothers Maze: draw a line from each baby to its own mother.

note.mistake: Children draw a straight line from start to goal across the grass, or follow the first road into a dead end and scribble out; on the babies and mothers maze they draw all three lines to the nearest mother.
note.words: Say, "Stay on the road, between the edges, like a tractor on the lane." Ask, "Is this road a dead end? Go back and try another way." Ask, "Who is this baby's mother? Find her road."
note.watch: The hen maze has a wide road to the corn with one short dead end, and a scarecrow, haystacks and a bird beside it; the horse maze has more branches on the way to the carrot; the babies and mothers maze has a chick, a calf and a foal at the top and a horse, a hen and a cow at the bottom.

lessons.check: Draws a line through a wide maze road without crossing the edges

themes.name: Fall and Forest Animals
themes.why: Fall outside: leaves change, the tree through the seasons, and the forest animals that get ready for winter.

lessons.title: Fall Forest Animal Word Cards
lessons.objective: Children name forest creatures (deer, raccoon, grasshopper, spider) and tell one thing each one does in fall.
lessons.routine: Take a fall walk and look for signs of animals: a squirrel burying a nut, a spider web, holes in leaves. With an adult watching, collect leaves, acorns and pine cones for a science table (acorns are small, so an adult stays at that table). Read aloud a picture book about forest animals in fall and find each card's animal in it.
week: Fall walk: look and listen for animals; collect leaves and pine cones with an adult watching.
Forest Word Cards: name the grasshopper, deer, raccoon and spider; the teacher cuts.
Science table: find the toy forest animals hiding among the leaves and name them.
Hop like a grasshopper, tiptoe like a deer, then clap: deer (1), rac-coon (2), grass-hop-per (3).
Tell a friend one forest animal and what it does to get ready for winter.

note.mistake: Children call the deer a "reindeer," the raccoon a "cat" or "bear," and the spider and grasshopper just "bugs"; some believe every forest animal sleeps all winter long.
note.words: Say, "This is a deer. Deer live in forests near us." Ask, "What does the raccoon have on its face? A mask!" Say, "A grasshopper jumps with its long back legs."
note.watch: The page shows four big cards: a grasshopper, a deer, a raccoon and a spider, each with its word under the picture. Watch who uses each animal's own name instead of "bug" or "dog."

lessons.check: Names a deer, a raccoon, a grasshopper and a spider and tells one fact

lessons.title: Fall Forest Animals: Which Is Heavier?
lessons.objective: Children compare two forest animals and decide which is heavier, thinking about the real animals.
lessons.routine: Use a balance scale with fall things: a pine cone and a leaf, a big rock and a feather, a small pumpkin (the teacher lifts it) and a pine cone. Children guess first, then watch which side goes down. Then they hold two things, one in each hand, and say which feels heavier. Talk about real forest animals: is a deer heavier than a squirrel?
week: Balance scale: a pine cone and a leaf, a rock and a feather; guess, then check.
Hand scales: hold two fall things, one in each hand, and say which is heavier.
Heavy or Light? page: circle the heavier forest animal in each pair.
Act it out: stomp like a heavy deer, scamper like a light mouse.
Make a heavy and light chart with the fall things we weighed.

note.mistake: Children circle the animal that looks bigger in its drawing, but both pictures sit in circles of the same size; others choose the animal they like or the one closer to their hand.
note.words: Ask, "In real life, which is heavier, a wolf or a squirrel?" Say, "The pictures are the same size. Think about the real animals." Ask, "Could you carry a deer? Could you carry a mouse?"
note.watch: The page shows three pairs of forest animals in equal circles (a wolf and a squirrel, a beaver and a mouse, a squirrel and a deer); the child circles the heavier one. Listen for a reason about the real animals, not the drawings.

lessons.check: Chooses the heavier of two real things or animals and says why

lessons.title: Fall and the Four Seasons: Our Tree
lessons.objective: Children watch a tree change with the seasons and match pictures to winter, spring, summer and fall.
lessons.routine: Adopt a tree on the playground. Visit it, feel the bark, look at the leaves and take a photo; come back to the same tree each season to compare. Inside, look at fall things (a pumpkin, red and yellow leaves) and talk about how the tree looks with snow on it, with new buds and with green leaves.
week: Adopt a playground tree: touch the bark, look at the leaves, take a photo.
Leaf sort: green, red, yellow and brown leaves; why do leaves change color in fall?
Four Seasons Sort page: lines from the skater, surfboard, pumpkin and lamb to the seasons.
Season dress-up: a scarf for winter, sunglasses for summer, a rain hat for spring, a sweater for fall.
Draw the Tree in Four Seasons: add leaves, snow, flowers or fruit to each tree.

note.mistake: Children think a tree with no leaves is dead, and on the sort many put the lamb in winter because it is woolly; the surfboard is new to most, and some put the pumpkin in summer because it is orange like the sun.
note.words: Ask, "What happens to our tree's leaves in fall?" Say, "In winter the tree rests. It is not dead." Ask, "When are baby lambs born? In spring." Say, "A surfboard is for the ocean in summer."
note.watch: The sort page shows a child skating, a surfboard, a pumpkin and a lamb above four boxes for winter, spring, summer and fall; the tree page has four bare trees labeled winter, spring, summer and fall for the child to draw on.

lessons.check: Matches a picture to each season and says how a tree looks in fall

lessons.title: Fall Leaves and Forest Pencil Paths
lessons.objective: Children trace a leaf and zigzag lines, then follow pencil paths to forest creatures.
lessons.routine: Make leaf rubbings: lay a real leaf under thin paper and rub it with the side of a peeled crayon, then trace the leaf's edge with a finger. Rake leaves into a pile with child rakes and walk zigzag paths through it. Draw zigzags in the air like the edge of a leaf.
week: Leaf rubbings: rub crayons over real leaves and trace the edges with a finger.
Rake leaves with child rakes and walk zigzag paths through the pile.
Autumn Leaves page: trace the leaf, the cloud, the sun and the zigzags.
Pencil Path Practice: trace to the grasshopper, the bee, the worm and the owl.
Glue real leaves on paper and draw zigzag grass under them.

note.mistake: Children round off the zigzag tips into bumps, or race through and miss the points; on the leaf they trace only the outline and skip the veins inside.
note.words: Say, "Stop at every tip of the zigzag, then turn." Ask, "Can you find the lines inside the leaf? Trace them too." Say, "Go slowly, like a leaf floating down."
note.watch: The Autumn Leaves page has a dashed leaf with veins, a cloud, a sun, a short zigzag and a long zigzag along the bottom; the pencil path page ends its four lines at a grasshopper, a bee, a worm and an owl. Look for sharp turns at each tip.

lessons.check: Traces a zigzag with sharp points and the outline of a leaf

themes.name: Construction and Tools
themes.why: Builders and their tools: hammers, wrenches and wheelbarrows, and who builds the houses we live in.

titles.picture-word-cards-easy-tools-k324-81: Tool Word Cards: Pliers, Hammer, Nail, Plunger
titles.picture-word-cards-easy-tools-bw-k324-82: Tool Word Cards to Color: Wheelbarrow, Saw, Gloves

lessons.title: Construction and Tools Word Cards
lessons.objective: Children name building tools (hammer, pliers, nail, plunger, wheelbarrow, saw, pickaxe, work gloves) and show what each one does.
lessons.routine: Open a construction zone with toy tools, hard hats, safety goggles and big cardboard boxes; children name each toy tool as they use it. Read aloud a picture book about building a house and point to each tool. Outside, children pull on real work gloves and carry blocks in a child-size wheelbarrow. Real saws and nails are for grown-ups only.
week: Construction zone opens: hard hats, goggles, toy tools and big boxes to build with.
Tool Word Cards: pliers, hammer, nail and plunger; act out how each one is used.
Work gloves and a child wheelbarrow outside: carry blocks to the building site.
Color the wheelbarrow, handsaw, pickaxe and gloves; clap gloves (1), pick-axe (2), wheel-bar-row (3).
Tool sort: tools for building, a tool for fixing a sink, and tools only grown-ups touch.

note.mistake: Children call every tool a hammer, and the plunger is new to most ("a stick with a cup"); some think a nail is a toy because it is small. Name each picture first, and keep real nails and saws out of children's reach.
note.words: Say, "Pliers pinch and hold." Ask, "What do we use a plunger for? To fix a stuck sink." Say, "Nails and saws are sharp. Only grown-ups use real ones."
note.watch: The color cards show pliers, a hammer, a nail and a plunger; the black-and-white cards show a wheelbarrow, a handsaw, a pickaxe and work gloves to color. Watch for the tool's name and a gesture that shows how it is used.

lessons.check: Names four tools and shows how each one is used

lessons.title: Construction and Tools: Same Number?
lessons.objective: Children count two groups of tools, even when one is spread out, and say whether they have the same number.
lessons.routine: Use toy tools or big building blocks. Put four toy hammers in a tight row and four spread far apart, and ask which row has more. Children count both rows, touching each tool, and find they are the same. Then they line the rows up one under one to check. Repeat with five and six blocks so children see that spreading things out does not change how many there are.
week: Tool count: line up toy hammers and count them, touching each one.
Spread them out: does the number change? Count again to find out.
One under one: line up two rows of blocks to see if one has more or they are the same.
Same Number? page: count each group of tools and circle the check if they match.
Partner game: one child builds a tight row, one a spread-out row; count and compare.

note.mistake: Children say the spread-out row has more because it is longer, without counting; after the spread-out game, others circle the check every time because they expect "the same." Writing the number is a challenge for the 5s; 3s can say it.
note.words: Ask, "This row looks longer. Does it have more? Let's count." Say, "Touch each tool once." Ask, "Five and five: is that the same number?"
note.watch: The page shows three pairs of rows of tools, one row neat and one spread out, with a box for each number and a check and an X to circle: six saws and six saws (the same), four plungers and three plungers, four hammers and five hammers. Watch one touch per tool.

lessons.check: Counts two rows of up to six things and says if they are the same number

lessons.title: Construction: Who Builds the House?
lessons.objective: Children match workers to what they make: the builder builds a house and the cook makes bread.
lessons.routine: Build a house as a class with big cardboard bricks and a paper roof; every child has a job (carrier, builder, painter). Talk about the builder's work. Then, after you check for allergies first, knead a little bread dough together and the adult bakes it in the school kitchen. Children say which worker made each thing: the house, the bread.
week: Class house: build with cardboard bricks; each child has a builder's job.
Who made it? Look at photos of a house, a loaf of bread, a sweater and a chair.
Who Makes It? page: draw lines from the builder and the cook to what they make.
Bread dough (check for allergies first): knead it, wash hands, no tasting; the adult bakes it.
School walk: find things builders made (walls, doors, windows, shelves).

note.mistake: Children think a house was "always there" or came from a store, and some match the cook to the house because both workers wear hats; others say the cook "does" the bread instead of making it.
note.words: Ask, "Who builds a house?" Say, "A builder builds houses. A cook or a baker makes bread." Ask, "What did our class build today?"
note.watch: The page shows two workers on the left (a builder holding a tool and a cook with a rolling pin) and two things on the right (a loaf of bread and a house); the child draws a line from each worker to what that worker makes.

lessons.check: Says who builds a house and who makes bread

lessons.title: Construction Tools: Pencil Paths and Tool Shapes
lessons.objective: Children trace pencil paths to tools and trace rows of circles, squares, triangles and diamonds.
lessons.routine: Tap golf tees into a block of craft foam with a wooden toy hammer while an adult sits at the table. Then lay painter's tape lines on the floor as a "building plan" and build block walls on them: a square wall, a triangle roof. Children run a finger along each tape line before they build.
week: Tool work: tap golf tees into foam with a wooden toy hammer (an adult at the table).
Building plan: lay painter's tape lines on the floor and build block walls on them.
Pencil Path Practice: trace lines to the flashlight, the hammer, the nail and the plunger.
Shape walls: build a square, a triangle and a diamond with long blocks.
Circles, Squares and More Shapes: trace each row of shapes from the dot.

note.mistake: Children press so hard at the corners of the squares and triangles that the paper tears, and on the pencil paths they slow down only at the end and run past the tool picture.
note.words: Say, "Builders measure and go slowly. Go slowly at the corners." Ask, "How many sides does the triangle have?" Say, "Stop when you reach the tool."
note.watch: The color pencil path page ends its lines at a flashlight, a hammer, a nail and a plunger; the black-and-white shape page has rows of circles, squares, triangles and diamonds with a wrench, a hammer, a screwdriver and a saw at the row ends.

lessons.check: Traces a square and a triangle with corners, from the starting dot

themes.name: Pets
themes.why: Pets and how we care for them, and how a pet is different from a wild animal.

lessons.title: Pets Word Cards: Cat, Chinchilla, Parrot, Frog
lessons.objective: Children name pets and say what every pet needs (food, water, a home and gentle hands).
lessons.routine: Set up a pet shop and vet in dramatic play with stuffed animals, empty food bowls, a pet bed and a toy stethoscope. If the class has a pet, children help the teacher feed it and then wash hands (no other animal handling). Read aloud a picture book about caring for a pet. Ask families to share a photo of a pet they have or would like.
week: Pet shop and vet open: care for stuffed pets with bowls, beds and brushes.
Pets Word Cards: the cat, chinchilla, parrot and frog; name the pictures first.
Class pet care, or a stuffed pet: feed it and fill the water with the teacher, then wash hands.
Pet photo share: children tell about a pet at home or one they would like.
Card game: say what each pet eats, then clap its name: cat (1), par-rot (2), chin-chil-la (3).

note.mistake: The chinchilla is new to almost every child (they say "mouse" or "bunny"), and some think a frog cannot be a pet; others say pets need only food and forget water, a clean home and gentle hands.
note.words: Say, "This is a chinchilla. It is a soft pet with big ears and a long tail." Ask, "What does a parrot need?" Say, "Some families keep a frog as a pet in a tank."
note.watch: The page shows four big cards (a cat, a chinchilla, a parrot and a frog), each with its word. Name the pictures first, then watch who can say what each pet needs.

lessons.check: Names four pets and one thing every pet needs

lessons.title: Pets: Connect the Dots 1 to 10 to Draw a Kitten
lessons.objective: Children count from 1 to 10 in order and connect the dots to finish a kitten.
lessons.routine: Set ten paper-plate pet bowls numbered 1 to 10 in a row. Children "feed" the pets by putting one large pom-pom in each bowl while counting aloud (an adult stays close). Then the teacher says a number and a child finds that bowl. Line up ten stuffed pets for the vet and count them from 1 to 10.
week: Feed the pets: one large pom-pom in each numbered bowl, from 1 to 10.
Find the bowl: the teacher says a number and a child finds that bowl.
Vet line: count the stuffed pets from 1 to 10 as they wait for the vet.
Dot-to-Dot 1 to 10: join the dots down the kitten's tail and along the ground under its paws.
Color the kitten and count its whiskers and paws.

note.mistake: Children trace over the kitten's drawn lines instead of joining the dots, or skip a dot where two sit close together under the paws; others start at 10 because it is on the left, where they start to read.
note.words: Say, "Start at the orange dot, 1, at the tip of the tail. Now find 2." Ask, "What number comes after 4?" Say, "The dots make the tail and the ground the kitten sits on."
note.watch: The page shows a sitting kitten; dots 1 to 4 run down its tail and dots 5 to 10 along the ground under its paws, starting at the orange dot, with a number strip from 1 to 10 at the bottom. Watch the child find each number before drawing to it.

lessons.check: Connects dots 1 to 10 in order and names the picture

lessons.title: Pets and Wild Animals
lessons.objective: Children sort animals into pets and wild animals and say why a wild animal does not live in a house.
lessons.routine: Set out two places: a pet bed with bowls (home) and a box of grass, rocks and branches (the wild). Children choose toy animals (a dog, a goldfish, a cat, a lion, a zebra, a bear) and put each one in its place, telling why. Talk about how pets need people to care for them, and wild animals find their own food.
week: Home or wild? Put toy animals on the pet bed or in the wild box and say why.
Pets need us: list what our class pet, or a stuffed pet, needs every day.
Pets and Wild Animals page: lines from the dog, zebra, goldfish and lion to the boxes.
Animal charades: act like a pet or a wild animal; friends say which one it is.
Pet care chart: food, water, a clean home and gentle hands.

note.mistake: Children say any animal they love can be a pet ("a lion can live in my room"), or put the goldfish with the wild animals because fish live in the ocean.
note.words: Ask, "Who feeds this animal, a person or the animal itself?" Say, "A goldfish lives in a bowl at home. It is a pet." Ask, "Why can't a lion be a pet?"
note.watch: The page shows a dog, a zebra, a goldfish and a lion above a Pets box and a Wild Animals box; the child draws a line from each animal's dot to a box. Listen for the reason the child gives.

lessons.check: Sorts four animals into pets and wild animals and says why

titles.maze-puzzles-k406: My First Maze: Help the Puppy Get to the Ball
titles.maze-puzzles-k406-6: My First Maze: Help the Kitten Get to the Milk

lessons.title: Pets Mazes: The Puppy's Ball and the Kitten's Milk
lessons.objective: Children draw a line along a wide maze road to help a puppy and a kitten reach their goal.
lessons.routine: Make a puppy path in the gym or outside with cones and hoops; children crawl through like puppies to fetch a soft ball. Then roll a ball along a bendy tape road and walk beside it. In a sand tray, children draw a road with a finger from a toy dog to a toy ball.
week: Puppy path: crawl through hoops and around cones to fetch a soft ball.
Tape road: roll a ball along a bendy tape road without leaving it.
My First Maze: help the puppy get to the ball along the wide road.
Sand tray roads: draw a finger road from a toy dog to a toy ball.
My First Maze: help the kitten get to the milk and turn back at dead ends.

note.mistake: Children trace along the road's edge instead of its middle, or turn into a side road toward a flower and get stuck; on the kitten maze many start at the milk and draw backward to the kitten.
note.words: Say, "Start where the puppy is, at the arrow." Ask, "Which road takes you to the ball?" Say, "Keep your line in the middle of the road."
note.watch: The puppy maze has a wide road from the puppy at the left to a soccer ball at the right, with a tree, a butterfly, a kitten, a bird and a tulip beside it; the kitten maze has a wide road through a farmyard from the kitten to a bottle of milk, with side roads that end.

lessons.check: Follows a wide maze road from start to goal and turns back at a dead end

themes.name: Thanksgiving
themes.why: Being thankful, harvest foods (pumpkins, corn, bread, pie) and the special days families keep.

lessons.title: Thanksgiving Word Cards: Pie, Pumpkin, Bread, Corn
lessons.objective: Children name harvest foods (pie, pumpkin, bread, corn) and say one thing they are thankful for.
lessons.routine: Check for allergies first. Bring a real pumpkin, an ear of corn in its husk and a loaf of bread, with a photo of a pie. Children feel, smell and describe each one and peel back the corn husk together. Read aloud a picture book about being thankful. Make a thankful chain: each child says, "I am thankful for..." and the teacher writes it on a paper strip.
week: Harvest basket: feel and describe a real pumpkin, an ear of corn and a loaf of bread.
Thanksgiving Word Cards: clap pie, bread, corn and pump-kin; which word takes two claps?
Peel the corn husk and look at the kernels; count a row of them together.
Thankful chain: each child says what they are thankful for; link the paper strips.
Taste bread or corn (check for allergies first) and describe it with the card words.

note.mistake: Children call the pie a "pizza" or "cake" and the corn a "banana" because of its shape; some think a pumpkin is only a decoration. "Thankful" is a new word: many say "I want..." when they mean "I am thankful for..."
note.words: Say, "Being thankful means being glad for something we have." Model, "I am thankful for my family." Ask, "What is inside the corn husk?" Say, "Pumpkins are food. We can make pie and soup from them."
note.watch: The page shows four big cards: a pie, a pumpkin, a loaf of bread and an ear of corn. Watch for the names and listen for a sentence that starts "I am thankful for."

lessons.check: Names pie, pumpkin, bread and corn and says one thing they are thankful for

lessons.title: Thanksgiving: Count and Trace 1 to 5
lessons.objective: Children count small groups of harvest things to 5 and trace the number that tells how many.
lessons.routine: Set up a harvest counting table with real things: one small pumpkin, two ears of mini corn, three gourds, four leaves and five pine cones. Children count each group, touching each one, and put the matching number card beside it. Then put five gourds in a basket and take them out one at a time, counting down together.
week: Harvest table: one pumpkin, two corn, three gourds, four leaves and five pine cones.
Match a number card to each group; touch and count to check.
Count and Trace page: count each row of harvest pictures and trace the number.
Make 5: put five gourds in a basket, then count them out one by one.
Air numbers: trace 1 to 5 in the air and on a friend's back.

note.mistake: Children trace the numbers without counting the pictures, or count the lone scarecrow as "one, two" because they touch it twice; many write 2 and 5 backward, which is normal at this age.
note.words: Ask, "How many pumpkins? Touch and count." Say, "The last number we say tells how many." Say, "Start the 5 at the top: down, around, and a hat on top."
note.watch: The page has five rows (one scarecrow, two hay bales, three pumpkins, four ears of corn and five pies), each with a number to look at and two to trace. Watch one touch per picture and the last number said.

lessons.check: Counts up to 5 harvest things, touching each one, and says how many

lessons.title: Thanksgiving and Family Traditions
lessons.objective: Children learn that families keep special days in different ways and match a tradition to each family picture.
lessons.routine: Invite families to share a special day they keep (a birthday, Thanksgiving, Diwali, Lunar New Year, an Eid meal) with a photo, a food or an object. Set up a special day table. Children look, touch and try what is offered (check for allergies first) and tell what their own family does on a special day.
week: Family tradition share: a family brings a photo or object from a special day.
