Special day table: look, touch and talk about each family's things.
Family Traditions page: lines from the pie and the red envelope to the family pictures.
Our thankful table: set a pretend table and say what we are thankful for.
Draw your family's special day and tell the class about it.

note.mistake: Children think every family keeps the same holidays theirs does, or that a special day they don't know is "not real"; some match the pie to the red-envelope picture because both families have food on the table.
note.words: Say, "Families celebrate in different ways, and all of them are special." Ask, "What does your family do on a special day?" Ask, "Which family has a pie on the table?"
note.watch: The page shows a pie and a red envelope on the left and two family pictures on the right: a family at a table with a turkey and pie, and a grandmother giving a child a red envelope under red lanterns. The child draws a line from each thing to its family.

lessons.check: Tells one way their family celebrates and listens to another family's way

lessons.title: Thanksgiving Pencil Paths: Turkey, Leaf and Pie
lessons.objective: Children trace straight, zigzag, bumpy, wavy and loopy pencil paths to harvest pictures.
lessons.routine: Draw chalk lines outside (straight, bumpy and wavy) and children walk them like turkeys, then hop the bumps. At the art table, children dip a cotton swab in paint and dot a straight line across the paper, then a wavy line. Finish with finger lines in a tray of sand.
week: Chalk lines outside: walk straight, bumpy and wavy paths like a turkey.
Cotton swab dots: paint a straight line of dots, then a wavy line.
Pencil Path Practice: trace to the turkey, the leaf, the scarecrow and the pie.
Finger paths in a tray of sand: straight, then bumpy, then wavy.
Pencil Path Review: trace five lines to the pie, scarecrow, bread, leaf and corn.

note.mistake: Children flatten the bumps into a straight line and skip the humps, and on the waves they go up and down in sharp points like a zigzag; some trace from the picture back to the dot.
note.words: Say, "Bumps go up and over, up and over, like a turkey hopping." Ask, "Are the waves pointy or round? Round." Say, "Begin at the orange dot every time."
note.watch: The first page ends its four lines at a turkey, a red leaf, a scarecrow and a pie; the review page has five lines (straight, waves, a zigzag, small bumps and big bumps) ending at a pie, a scarecrow, bread, a leaf and corn. Look for round bumps and pointy zigzags.

lessons.check: Traces bumpy and wavy lines from the dot without turning them into zigzags

themes.name: Toys
themes.why: Our toys: sorting them, finding the longest, and how we push and pull toys to make them move.

lessons.title: Toys: Cut, Sort and Paste Robots, Boats and Rockets
lessons.objective: Children sort toy pictures into groups of the same kind and say why each one belongs there.
lessons.routine: Tip a basket of real toys onto the rug (cars, blocks, dolls, balls, toy boats). Children sort them into hoops by kind and say the rule: "All the balls go here." Sort again: toys that roll and toys that don't. Read aloud a picture book about a favorite toy. Before the page, children snip paper strips with child-safe scissors.
week: Toy sort on the rug: put real toys into hoops by kind and say the rule.
Sort again: toys that roll and toys that don't roll.
Snip practice: cut strips of paper with child-safe scissors.
Cut, Sort and Paste page: cut out the robots, boats and rockets and glue each in its column.
Tell a friend how you sorted, then build with the toys from one group.

note.mistake: Children glue a picture wherever there is space or split two of a kind into different columns; cutting the strip into squares is hard, and many cut through the middle of a picture.
note.words: Ask, "What toy is at the top of this column? Find all the ones that match it." Say, "Cut on the line between the pictures." Ask, "Why does this boat go here?"
note.watch: The page has three columns topped by a robot, a boat and a rocket, with two boxes in each, and a strip of six pictures (robots, boats and rockets) to cut out at the bottom. Help 3s cut the strip apart; watch the sorting.

lessons.check: Sorts toys by kind and tells the rule for the group

lessons.title: Toys: Long and Short
lessons.objective: Children compare toy vehicles and find the longest one in each row.
lessons.routine: Line up real toy cars, trucks and trains of different lengths on a table. Children set two side by side with the back ends lined up to see which is longer. Build a long cube train and a short cube train and compare them. Then find the longest ribbon or jump rope laid on the floor and walk along it.
week: Toy cars side by side: line up the back ends and find the longest car.
Cube trains: build a long train and a short train and compare them.
Ribbons on the floor: find the longest one and walk along it.
Long and Short page: circle the longest toy in each row.
Lay block towers on their side and find which one is longest.

note.mistake: Children choose the toy that looks tallest instead of the longest, or compare real toys without lining up the ends. On the page the four toys in a row are bigger and smaller copies of one toy, so the longest is also the biggest: ask how they know.
note.words: Ask, "Which one is the longest? Put the ends together to check." Say, "Long means from one end to the other end." Ask, "Which plane is longer, this one or that one?"
note.watch: The page has three rows of four toys (yellow and red airplanes, dump trucks and green cars), bigger and smaller copies of one toy; the child circles the longest in each row. Ask the child to show "from one end to the other end" with two fingers.

lessons.check: Finds the longest of four toys by lining up their ends

lessons.title: Toys: Push or Pull?
lessons.objective: Children tell a push from a pull by moving toys, and match pictures to push or pull.
lessons.routine: Bring toys that move: a wagon, a toy train with a string, a toy shopping cart, a ball, and a box with a rope tied to it. Children move each one and say "I push it" or "I pull it." Mark two areas with signs, push toys and pull toys. Try the wagon both ways: from behind it is a push, from the front with the handle it is a pull.
week: Moving toys: push the shopping cart, pull the wagon, and say which you did.
Rope or hands? Move a box with a rope, then without one.
Push or Pull? page: lines from the sled, the cart, the train and the truck to push or pull.
Push and pull walk: find doors, drawers and chairs that we push or pull.
Push a ball and pull a wagon outside; tell a friend which was harder.

note.mistake: Children say "push" for everything that moves forward and mix up where the person stands: walking in front with a rope is a pull. The toy train has the person behind it, which many still call a pull.
note.words: Ask, "Is the person in front pulling, or behind pushing?" Say, "Pull brings it toward you. Push moves it away from you." Ask, "Where is the rope?"
note.watch: The page shows four pictures with arrows: a person pulling a red sled by a rope, a person pushing a shopping cart, a person pushing a toy train, and a person pulling a toy dump truck by a rope. The child draws a line from each to push or pull.

lessons.check: Shows a push and a pull with a toy and says which is which

titles.pre-writing-easy-toys-k236-83: Pencil Path Practice: Toys in Color
titles.pre-writing-easy-toys-bw-k236-84: Pencil Path Practice: Toys to Color

lessons.title: Toys Pencil Paths in Color and Black and White
lessons.objective: Children trace straight, zigzag, bumpy and wavy pencil paths to toys.
lessons.routine: Drive toy cars along tape roads on the floor: a straight road, a zigzag road and a wavy road. Then roll play-dough snakes and bend them into the same shapes. Children draw a road for their toy car on a whiteboard with a marker and drive it.
week: Tape roads: drive toy cars along straight, zigzag and wavy roads.
Play-dough snakes: bend them into zigzags and waves.
Pencil Path Practice: trace lines to the plane, the bike, the doll and the blocks.
Whiteboard roads: draw a road for your toy car and drive it.
Pencil Path Practice to color: trace to the train, the guitar, the car and the plane.

note.mistake: Children trace with the wrist lifted off the table, so the lines wander; on the black-and-white page they start coloring the toys before the lines are done, and the waves turn into scribbles.
note.words: Say, "Drive your crayon like a car on the road. Stay on the dashes." Ask, "Which toy is at the end of the wavy road?" Say, "Lines first, coloring last."
note.watch: The color page ends its lines at a toy plane, a bike, a doll and a stack of blocks; the black-and-white page ends at a toy train, a guitar, a car and a plane to color. Look at the wrist on the table and dash-by-dash tracing.

lessons.check: Traces four kinds of lines from the dot to the toy

themes.name: Cooking and Baking
themes.why: The kitchen and the bakery: baked foods, kitchen tools, and what is hot and what is cold.

titles.picture-word-cards-easy-bakery-k324-18: Bakery Word Cards: Pie, Cookie, Bagel, Croissant
titles.picture-word-cards-kitchen-tools-k324-15: Kitchen Word Cards: Refrigerator, Apron, Teapot, Oven

lessons.title: Cooking and Baking Word Cards: Bakery and Kitchen
lessons.objective: Children name baked foods and kitchen things (pie, cookie, bagel, croissant, refrigerator, apron, blender, oven) and say what each is for.
lessons.routine: Check for allergies first. Bake simple muffins together: children measure, pour and stir (no tasting raw batter), and the adult works the oven while children stand back. Read aloud a picture book about baking. Open a bakery and kitchen in dramatic play with play food, an apron, a teapot and unbreakable pots, where children sell "bagels" and "croissants."
week: Bake (check for allergies first): measure, pour and stir; no tasting raw batter; the adult runs the oven.
Bakery Word Cards: name the pie, cookie, bagel and croissant.
Pretend bakery: sell play bagels, croissants and cookies to friends.
Kitchen Word Cards: bottle, jar, refrigerator, apron, teapot, blender, pot and oven; find each one.
Bakery game: name a card and clap it: pot (1), ap-ron (2), re-frig-er-a-tor (5).

note.mistake: Children call every baked thing "bread" or "cake," and the croissant and bagel are new words ("the curvy bread," "the donut"); on the kitchen cards the blender gets called a "mixer" and the refrigerator "the fridge," which is right too.
note.words: Say, "A bagel has a hole like a donut, but it is bread." Ask, "Where do we keep the milk cold? In the refrigerator." Say, "An apron keeps our clothes clean when we cook."
note.watch: The bakery cards show a pie, a cookie, a bagel and a croissant; the kitchen page has eight smaller cards: a bottle, a jar, a refrigerator, an apron, a teapot, a blender, a pot and an oven. Watch who uses the new words bagel, croissant and apron in play.

lessons.check: Names two baked foods and two kitchen things

lessons.title: Cooking and Baking: Which Treat Is Third?
lessons.objective: Children count places in a row of baked foods from the flag and find first, next and last.
lessons.routine: Line up five play baked foods on a tray with a paper flag at one end: a bun, a cookie, a muffin, a slice of pie and a bagel. Children count places from the flag: first, second, third. Then five children each hold a play food and stand in a bakery line; a customer asks, "May I have the third one?" and the class counts to find it.
week: Bakery tray: count five play foods from the flag: first, second, third.
Bakery line: a customer asks for the second or the fourth treat; the class counts to find it.
Baking steps: what did we do first, next and last when we made muffins?
Ordinal Numbers page: the teacher reads each chip; children count from the flag and mark.
Line up to wash hands and say your place in the bakery line.

note.mistake: Children point to the treat they would like to eat instead of counting, or count the flag; when a chip says "3rd," some look for three of something on the page.
note.words: Say, "The flag shows where we start. First, second, third." Ask, "Which treat is first? Which is last?" Read, "This chip says fifth with a circle. Count five from the flag and circle it."
note.watch: The page has three rows of five baked foods (pies, a bun, a cupcake, a muffin, cake slices, a pretzel, a bagel, toast) with a flag at the left and two chips under each row. Read each chip aloud; 3s may find first and last.

lessons.check: Counts places from the front to find the third of five things

lessons.title: Cooking and Baking: Hot and Cold
lessons.objective: Children sort things into hot and cold and learn that some kitchen things are too hot to touch.
lessons.routine: Feel the difference safely: an ice cube in a bowl and a cup of warm (not hot) water. Walk the kitchen with the cook: the oven and stove get hot, only grown-ups use them, and we stand back. Watch ice melt on a plate near a sunny window. Then sort pictures of foods into a "fridge" box and an "oven" box.
week: Feel safely: an ice cube and a cup of warm water; which is cold, which is warm?
Kitchen safety walk: the oven and stove are hot; we stand back and grown-ups use them.
Hot and Cold page: lines from the snowman, the oven, the ice and the grill to the boxes.
Melt watch: ice on a plate in the sun and ice in the shade; which melts first?
Fridge or oven? Sort food pictures into a cold box and a hot box.

note.mistake: Children think an oven is safe to touch when they see no flame, and some put the snowman under hot because snowmen "melt." The rule is simple: never touch, ask a grown-up.
note.words: Ask, "Is an oven hot or cold when it is on?" Say, "Hot things can hurt us. We ask a grown-up." Ask, "Where does the ice go, hot or cold?"
note.watch: The page shows a snowman, an oven, a block of ice and a grill above a Hot box and a Cold box; the child draws a line from each dot to a box. Listen for "too hot to touch."

lessons.check: Sorts hot and cold things and says not to touch the hot ones

lessons.title: Cooking and Baking: Swirls and Pencil Paths
lessons.objective: Children trace spirals and loops like cinnamon rolls and steam, and follow pencil paths to bakery and kitchen pictures.
lessons.routine: Roll play-dough snakes and curl them into cinnamon-roll spirals, then twist them into pretzels. Children stir pretend batter (sand and water) in big circles with an unbreakable spatula and a whisk. Draw spirals in shaving cream on the table, starting at the outside and curling in to the middle, the way the page does.
week: Play-dough cinnamon rolls: roll a snake and curl it into a spiral.
Shaving-cream spirals: start at the outside and curl in to the middle, like the page.
Bakery Swirls page: trace the big spiral, the steam loops and the cupcake swirl.
Pencil Path Practice: trace lines to the pie, the bun, the pretzel and the cake.
Pencil Path Practice: trace lines to the mixer, the oven, the pot and the cake dome.

note.mistake: Children draw a spiral as circles inside circles, lifting the crayon each time, or go round the wrong way and run out of room; the steam loops are small, and many turn them into scribbles.
note.words: Say, "Start at the outside dot and curl in, round and round, like a cinnamon roll." Ask, "Did your crayon lift?" Say, "Little loops, like steam from a hot cup."
note.watch: The Bakery Swirls page has a big spiral, two steam loops over a teacup and a swirl on a cupcake; the bakery pencil paths end at a pie, a bun, a pretzel and a cake; the kitchen paths end at a mixer, an oven, a pot and a covered cake dome.

lessons.check: Traces a spiral round and round without lifting

themes.name: Space
themes.why: The sky by day and by night in the longest nights of the year: sun, moon, stars, planets and rockets.

lessons.title: Space Words: Galaxy, Planet, Rocket
lessons.objective: Children say three space words (galaxy, planet, rocket), hear their first sounds and trace them with a finger, then a crayon.
lessons.routine: Darken the room and shine a flashlight on a small ball moon and a big ball earth. Make cardboard-tube telescopes and find planet and rocket pictures taped to the ceiling. Read aloud a picture book about space and stop at each rocket and planet. Write galaxy, planet and rocket big on chart paper; children trace each word with a finger while the class says it slowly.
week: Flashlight sky: in the dark room, shine a light on a ball moon and a big ball earth.
Space read-aloud, then trace galaxy, planet and rocket with a finger on the chart.
Tube telescopes: find the pictures on the ceiling and clap rock-et (2), plan-et (2), gal-ax-y (3).
Trace and Write the Words page: say each word, then trace it (writing it is a challenge for the 5s).
First sounds: rocket starts with /r/, planet with /p/; find a friend whose name starts the same.

note.mistake: Children trace the dashed letters from right to left or start each letter at the bottom, and some write their own name instead of the word. For 3s and young 4s the words are a stretch: they say the word and trace its first letter.
note.words: Say, "This word says rocket. Rocket starts with /r/." Ask, "What is this picture? A planet, very far away in space." Say, "Start each letter at the top, and go from left to right."
note.watch: The page has three rows (a galaxy, a ringed planet and a rocket), each with the word to look at, the same word dashed to trace and empty lines to write it. Writing is a challenge for the 5s; 3s name the picture and trace the first letter.

lessons.check: Says galaxy, planet and rocket and names the first sound of rocket

lessons.title: Space: Count Back From 10 to Blast Off
lessons.objective: Children count back from 10 to 1 and connect the dots in that order to finish a rocket.
lessons.routine: Build a cardboard box rocket. Children crouch beside it, count back together from 10 to 1 and "blast off" with a jump. Lay ten number cards in a row on the floor and children step backward from 10 to 1. Build a tower of ten cubes and take one cube off for each number the class says.
week: Box rocket blast off: count back from 10 to 1 together, then jump.
Step back: walk backward on number cards from 10 down to 1.
Cube tower: start with ten and take one off for each number we say.
Dot-to-Dot Count Back: start at 10 and connect the dots down to 1 to finish the rocket.
Rocket races: count back from 5 or from 10 before each race on the playground.

note.mistake: Children start the dot-to-dot at 1 out of habit, or count back "10, 9, 8, 7, 5" and skip a number; most 3s can count back only from 5, and that is fine.
note.words: Say, "We start at 10 and count down: 10, 9, 8." Ask, "What comes before 7?" Say, "When we get to 1, the rocket blasts off!"
note.watch: The page shows a rocket whose top and sides are made by dots numbered 10 down to 1, with 10 at the orange dot and a number strip from 10 to 1 at the bottom. Counting back is a challenge for the 5s: 3s join the dots as the teacher calls the numbers.

lessons.check: Counts back from 10 (or from 5) without skipping a number

lessons.title: Space: The Day Sky and the Night Sky
lessons.objective: Children sort things into the day sky and the night sky (the sun, a star, a comet, a bird).
lessons.routine: Go outside on a clear morning and look at the day sky for clouds, birds and sometimes the moon (never look straight at the sun). Inside, turn off the lights and cover the ceiling lights with paper stars; children lie on the rug and look at the "night sky." Each child makes a day half and a night half on paper with sun and star stickers.
week: Day sky walk: look for clouds, birds and the moon (never look at the sun).
Night sky inside: lights off, paper stars on the ceiling; lie down and look up.
Day and Night page: lines from the sun, the comet, the bird and the star to the boxes.
Day and night sort: pajamas, a pillow, sunglasses and a lunch box.
Make a day half and a night half on paper with sun and star stickers.

note.mistake: Children think the sun "turns off" at night and that stars are made each evening; many put the bird in the night box because birds sleep in trees, and the comet is new to almost everyone.
note.words: Ask, "When do we see the sun?" Say, "The stars are always there. We see them when it is dark." Ask, "When does a bird fly, in the day or at night?" Say, "A comet is a bright light with a long tail."
note.watch: The page shows a sun, a comet, a bird and a star above a Day box and a Night box; the child draws a line from each picture's dot to a box. Name the comet first, then listen for reasons that use light and dark.

lessons.check: Sorts the sun, a star and a bird into day and night

titles.picture-tracing-easy-k418-6: Picture Tracing: Rocket to the Stars
titles.picture-tracing-easy-k424-3: Spirals and Loops to Trace: Space Spirals

lessons.title: Space Tracing: Rockets, Stars and Spirals
lessons.objective: Children trace a rocket, stars and planets, and spirals that go round and round.
lessons.routine: Press star and circle cookie cutters into play-dough and trace the shapes with a finger. Spin slowly on the rug like planets, then draw spirals in the air and on a whiteboard. Paint a tall rocket at the easel with long up-and-down strokes.
week: Play-dough stars and planets with cookie cutters; trace the edges with a finger.
Planet spins on the rug, then spirals in the air and on a whiteboard.
Rocket to the Stars page: trace the rocket, the planet, the stars and the flying saucer.
Space Spirals page: trace the big spiral round and round, then the loops.
My First Tracing: trace the big rocket in its circle, slowly, all the way round.

note.mistake: Children trace the five-pointed stars as blobs and miss the points, and on the spiral they jump from ring to ring; on the big rocket some press so hard the crayon breaks.
note.words: Say, "Stars have points: up, down, up, down." Ask, "Can you go round and round without lifting?" Say, "Hold the crayon gently, like a little bird."
note.watch: The rocket page has a dashed rocket, a ringed planet, a flying saucer and four stars; the spiral page has one big spiral among stars and two loopy paths to a saucer and a star; the last page has one big rocket inside a circle with a moon and stars.

lessons.check: Traces a star's points and a spiral without lifting the crayon

themes.name: Winter
themes.why: Snow, ice and cold (week 1) and the animals that live where it is always cold, penguins, seals and walruses (week 2).

titles.picture-word-cards-winter-k324-194: Winter Word Cards: Cabin, Igloo, Skating, Snowman
titles.picture-word-cards-easy-winter-k324-97: Winter Word Cards: Walrus, Earmuffs, Boots, Penguin

lessons.title: Winter Word Cards: Snow, Ice and Cold-Weather Animals
lessons.objective: Children name winter things and animals of the cold (cabin, sweater, igloo, snowman, walrus, penguin, seal) and use the words in a sentence.
lessons.routine: Bring winter inside: a bin of real snow or crushed ice with mittens to wear, toy penguins, seals and a walrus, and a cabin made from a box. Children build a tiny snowman in the bin and tell a friend about it. Read aloud a picture book about a snowy day. Show photos of skaters and skiers, of penguins near the South Pole and of walruses near the North Pole.
week: Snow bin: play in real snow or crushed ice wearing mittens; name what we feel.
Winter Word Cards: cabin, fireplace, sweater, skating, igloo, skiing, seal and snowman.
Paper-plate skating on the rug; pretend skiing with arms and knees.
Build a small snowman in the snow bin and tell each step to a friend.
Card hunt: find the hidden winter cards and clap each name: seal (1), ig-loo (2), snow-man (2).
Cold-animal trays: penguins on one, a walrus and seals on the other; they live far apart.
Winter Word Cards: walrus, earmuffs, boots and penguin.
Waddle like a penguin and flop like a seal, naming the animal as you move.
Sort the winter cards: animals in one pile, things we wear or use in another.
Winter word show: each child holds a card and says a sentence about it.

note.mistake: Children call the walrus and the seal both "seal," the igloo a "snow house" (accept it, then name it) and the fireplace an "oven"; skating and skiing get mixed up.
note.words: Say, "A walrus has long tusks. A seal does not." Ask, "Do you skate on ice or ski on snow?" Say, "An igloo is a house made of blocks of snow."
note.watch: The first page has eight cards (a cabin, a fireplace, a sweater, a skater, an igloo, a skier, a seal and a snowman); the second has four big cards (a walrus, earmuffs, boots and a penguin). Listen for "walrus" and "seal" told apart.

lessons.check: Names four winter things and two animals that live in the cold

lessons.title: Winter: Count and Trace 1 to 5
lessons.objective: Children count winter pictures to 5 and trace the number that tells how many.
lessons.routine: Count real winter things: one mitten, two scarves, three hats, four paper snowflakes and five cotton-ball snowballs. Children set each group on a mat with its number card. Play snowball toss: toss cotton balls into a bucket and count how many went in, up to five. Roll play-dough snowmen and count the balls in each.
week: Winter count: one mitten, two scarves, three hats, four snowflakes, five snowballs.
Match a number card to each winter group; touch and count to check.
Snowball toss: toss cotton balls into a bucket and count how many went in.
Play-dough snowmen: roll the balls and count them; make one with three.
Count and Trace page: count each row of winter pictures and trace the number.
Mitten match: count the pairs of mittens hanging on the line.
Snowflakes on the window: the teacher folds and cuts; children count up to five.
Number hunt: find the numbers 1 to 5 on paper snowflakes hidden in the room.
Count the penguins: line up toy penguins and count to five.
Count and Trace again with a friend, touching each picture before tracing.

note.mistake: Children count the small pictures too fast and touch one twice, most often the four snowflakes in a row; others trace the number before counting and just copy its shape.
note.words: Say, "Count first, then trace." Ask, "How many snowflakes? Touch each one." Say, "Four: down, across, and one long line down."
note.watch: The page has five rows (one snowboarder, two pink coats, three walruses, four snowflakes and five fireplaces), each with a number to look at and two to trace. The pictures are small; let the child touch each one with a finger before tracing.

lessons.check: Counts up to 5 winter pictures and traces the matching number

titles.science-sort-easy-k724-4: Hot and Cold Places: Ball, Sled, Swimsuit, Flip-Flops
titles.science-sort-easy-k724-5: Hot and Cold Places: Coat, Mittens, Ball, Hat

lessons.title: Winter: Hot Places and Cold Places
lessons.objective: Children match things people use to a snowy place or a sunny beach, and talk about how the cold changes what we wear and do.
lessons.routine: Set up two corners: a cold place with blankets, mittens, hats and a sled, and a hot place with a beach towel, sunglasses and a sun hat. Children dress for one place and act out a day there. Put a cup of water outside or in the freezer overnight and look at the ice together the next morning.
week: Freeze it: put a cup of water outside or in the freezer overnight.
Check the ice; feel cold with mittens on and with mittens off.
Cold corner and hot corner: dress for each and act out a day there.
Hot Places, Cold Places page: lines from the ball, the sled, the swimsuit and the flip-flops.
Penguins and seals: why are they comfortable in the cold?
Ice blocks: freeze toy animals in ice and melt them with warm water.
Animal coats: feel wool, a feather and fleece; which keeps an animal warm?
Hot Places, Cold Places page: lines from the coat, the mittens, the beach ball and the hat.
Pack a bag: choose what to bring to the snowy place and to the beach.
Share: one thing you would do in the cold and one thing in the heat.

note.mistake: Children say we wear coats "because it's winter," not because it is cold, and think the beach is never chilly; some send the wool hat to the beach because "a hat is for the sun."
note.words: Ask, "Would you wear this in the snow or at the beach?" Say, "We wear a coat to keep warm when it is cold." Ask, "Is this a sun hat or a warm hat?"
note.watch: Both pages show a snowy mountain place with a cabin and a sunny beach place; the first has a beach ball, a sled, a swimsuit and flip-flops to match, the second a pink coat, green mittens, a beach ball and a wool hat. Listen to the reasons children give.

lessons.check: Matches clothes and toys to a cold place or a hot place and says why

titles.picture-tracing-easy-k418-4: Picture Tracing: Penguins on the Ice

lessons.title: Winter Tracing: Snowman Shapes and Penguins on Ice
lessons.objective: Children trace a snowman made of shapes and a scene of penguins and a seal on the ice.
lessons.routine: Build a snowman outside, or with play-dough, from three balls of different sizes, then trace circles in the snow with a stick or in a tray of salt with a finger. Draw icy lines in shaving cream ("fake snow") and waddle along a tape line like penguins, feet close together.
week: Snowman building: three balls from big to small, outside or with play-dough.
Snow drawing: circles with a stick in the snow, or with a finger in a salt tray.
The Shape Snowman page: trace the circles, the square and the triangle; color the circles.
Penguin waddle along a tape line, feet close together and arms at our sides.
Shaving-cream snow: draw circles and wavy lines with a finger.
Penguins on the Ice page: trace the igloo, the seal, the two penguins and the ice.
Cotton-ball snow: glue cotton balls onto the traced snowman.
Ice cracks: draw zigzag cracks and wavy water with chalk on dark paper.
Color the penguin page and tell a friend what the penguins are doing.
Make a winter picture with circles, triangles and wavy lines.

note.mistake: Children trace the snowman's circles as one long oval and forget the square hat and the triangle; on the penguin page they trace only the penguins and leave out the igloo and the wavy line of the water.
note.words: Say, "Three circles, one on top of another, then a square hat." Ask, "Did you trace the igloo too?" Say, "Follow the wavy line where the water meets the ice."
note.watch: The snowman page has a dashed square hat, three circles for the body, and one more circle and a triangle beside it; the penguin page shows an igloo, a seal, two penguins, a sun and a wavy line of water under the ice. Look for whole shapes that close.

lessons.check: Traces circles that close and a whole winter picture along the dashes

themes.name: Clothing
themes.why: What we wear and why: mittens and coats for winter, shorts and swimsuits for summer, getting dressed by myself.

titles.picture-word-cards-clothing-k324-131: Clothing Word Cards: Coat, Pants, Jumpsuit, Slippers
titles.picture-word-cards-apparel-bw-k324-114: Clothing Word Cards to Color: Boots, Dress, Mittens

lessons.title: Clothing Word Cards: What We Wear
lessons.objective: Children name pieces of clothing (coat, pants, leggings, slippers, boots, dress, shorts, mittens) and say when they wear them.
lessons.routine: Fill a dress-up basket with real clothes in big sizes: a coat, pants, leggings, slippers, a hat, a dress, shorts and mittens. Children put each one on over their own clothes and say what it is and when they wear it. Read aloud a picture book about getting dressed for the weather. Hang a clothesline and clip a real piece of clothing beside each card.
week: Dress-up basket: put on a coat, a hat and mittens over our clothes and name them.
Clothing Word Cards: slippers, belt, jumpsuit, coat, pants, leggings, hat and tie.
Clothesline: clip real clothes on a line and say a word for each one.
Clothing Word Cards to color: necktie, sock, boots, dress, shorts, mittens, hat and jacket.
Get-dressed game: clap each piece as you put it on: hat (1), mit-tens (2), leg-gings (2).

note.mistake: Children call every kind of pants "pants" (leggings and the jumpsuit too) and every top a "shirt"; the necktie and the belt are grown-up clothes many 4-year-olds have no word for, and mittens and gloves get mixed up.
note.words: Say, "Leggings are soft, stretchy pants." Ask, "Is a jumpsuit pants or a shirt? It is both in one piece!" Say, "Mittens keep all our fingers together. Gloves have a place for each finger."
note.watch: The color page has eight cards (slippers, a belt, a green jumpsuit, a red coat, yellow pants, leggings, a hat and a tie); the black-and-white page has eight to color (a necktie, a sock, boots, a dress, shorts, mittens, a hat and a jacket). Listen for a word for each piece and when the child wears it.

lessons.check: Names six pieces of clothing and says when to wear one of them

lessons.title: Clothing: Match Them Up, More or the Same
lessons.objective: Children match clothes one to one between two rows and say which row has more, or that they are the same.
lessons.routine: Tip a laundry basket of socks onto the rug and match them into pairs; any sock left over has no partner. Hang hats and mittens in two rows on a clothesline and pair each hat with a mitten to find the extras. Then share caps and scarves between two friends: "One for you, one for me."
week: Sock pairs: match the socks from a laundry basket; which sock has no partner?
Clothesline rows: pair each hat with a mitten and find the extras.
One for you, one for me: share caps and scarves between two friends.
Match Them Up page: draw a line from each picture to a partner; circle the row with more.
Two rows of clothes on the line: color the star when every one has a partner.

note.mistake: Children draw two lines to one partner or say the longer-looking row has more; on the row of ten jackets and ten coats many lose track halfway and circle a row instead of coloring the star. Watches are not clothes to some children: name the pictures first.
note.words: Say, "One line to one partner, like socks in pairs." Ask, "Is anyone left without a partner? That row has more." Say, "If everyone has a partner, color the star."
note.watch: The page has five pairs of rows of small black-and-white clothes: five T-shirts and seven boots, five watches and two hats, ten jackets and ten coats (the same), three pairs of mittens and five shorts, five dresses and four caps. The rows run up to ten, so 3s do rows 2, 4 and 5.

lessons.check: Matches two rows one to one and says which has more or that they are the same

lessons.title: Clothing for Summer and Winter
lessons.objective: Children sort clothes into summer clothes and winter clothes and say how clothes keep us warm or cool.
lessons.routine: Put a coat, boots, a cap and a swimsuit in a basket. Children try on the coat and boots and say how they feel (warm, heavy, puffy). Before going outside each day, look at the weather together and decide what we need to wear. Make a summer and winter clothing mural with pictures cut from catalogs.
week: Weather check at the door: what do we need to wear outside today?
Try on a coat and boots, then a sun hat: how does each one feel?
Summer and Winter Clothes page: lines from the coat, the cap, the boots and the swimsuit.
Clothing mural: summer clothes on the sun side, winter clothes on the snow side.
Pack a suitcase for a snowy trip and another for a beach trip.

note.mistake: Children put the cap under winter because it is a hat, and many think boots are only for snow (rain boots too); some say we wear a coat because it is "big," not because it keeps us warm.
note.words: Ask, "Do you wear a swimsuit when it is hot or cold?" Say, "A coat keeps our body warm." Ask, "Could this cap go to the beach? Why?"
note.watch: The page shows a red coat, a blue cap, brown boots and a swimsuit above a Summer box and a Winter box; the child draws a line from each dot. Accept the cap in either box when the child gives a reason.

lessons.check: Sorts four pieces of clothing into summer and winter and says why

lessons.title: Clothing Pencil Paths: Lines to Hats and Socks
lessons.objective: Children trace pencil paths, zigzags and a square wave to pieces of clothing, and practice the small moves of getting dressed.
lessons.routine: Practice the hand work of getting dressed on a dressing board: pull a zipper, push a big button through its hole, press a snap and lace a shoe card. Clip clothespins onto a line of socks and mittens. Lay long scarves on the floor in wavy and zigzag shapes and walk beside them.
week: Dressing board: zip, button, snap and lace with our fingers.
Clothespin line: clip socks and mittens onto a string with clothespins.
Pencil Path Practice: trace lines to the scarf, the cap, the pajamas and the T-shirt.
Scarf paths: lay scarves in wavy and zigzag shapes and walk beside them.
Straight Lines and Zigzags: trace to the tie, the sock and the glasses, then the square wave.

note.mistake: On the square wave children slant the up and down strokes into a zigzag, and on the zigzags they lift the crayon at each point. Buttons and zippers are hard for 3s: the practice matters more than finishing.
note.words: Say, "Square wave: up, across, down, across, like the top of a castle." Ask, "Where does this line take you? To the hat." Say, "Pinch the clothespin like a crocodile's mouth."
note.watch: The color page ends its lines at a scarf, a cap, red pajamas and a green T-shirt; the black-and-white page has straight lines and zigzags to a tie, a sock and glasses, and a square-wave line to a hat. Look for straight up-and-down strokes on the square wave.

lessons.check: Traces zigzags and a square wave with corners, and zips or buttons with help

themes.name: Healthy Eating
themes.why: A good breakfast and everyday foods that help us grow, and the sometimes foods.

lessons.title: Healthy Eating: Breakfast Word Cards
lessons.objective: Children name breakfast foods (pancake, grapefruit, raspberry, porridge) and tell what they eat in the morning.
lessons.routine: Check for allergies first. Have a class breakfast tasting: a small piece of pancake, raspberries cut in half and warm oatmeal (porridge). Children name each food and say whether it is sweet, sour or soft. Read aloud a picture book about breakfast. Graph what everyone ate for breakfast and open a breakfast cafe in dramatic play with play food.
week: Breakfast talk: what did you eat this morning? Draw it on a paper plate.
Breakfast Word Cards: pancake, grapefruit, raspberry and porridge.
Tasting (check for allergies first): pancake, raspberries and porridge; sweet, sour or soft?
Breakfast cafe: order with the card words and clap them: pan-cake (2), rasp-ber-ry (3).
Breakfast graph: put your picture in the row of the breakfast you like best.

note.mistake: Children call porridge "soup" or "cereal" and the grapefruit an "orange"; some say breakfast must be cereal, so a friend's rice or tortilla breakfast sounds "wrong" to them.
note.words: Say, "Porridge is warm oatmeal. Some families call it hot cereal." Ask, "Is a grapefruit sweet or sour?" Say, "Families eat many different breakfasts, and they are all breakfast."
note.watch: The page shows four big cards: a pancake, half a grapefruit, a raspberry and a bowl of porridge. Listen for the names and for a describing word (sweet, sour, warm, soft).

lessons.check: Names four breakfast foods and describes one by its taste

lessons.title: Healthy Eating: Count and Trace Breakfast Foods
lessons.objective: Children count breakfast foods up to 5 and trace the number that tells how many.
lessons.routine: Set a play breakfast table: one strip of play bacon, two blueberries, three croissants, four jam jars and five muffins. Children count each group onto a plate and put the number card next to it. At snack, after you check for allergies first, each child counts out up to five apple slices before eating.
week: Play breakfast table: count one, two, three, four and five foods onto plates.
Number card match: put the right card by each plate and count to check.
Snack count (check for allergies first): count out up to five apple slices.
Count and Trace page: count each row of breakfast foods and trace the number.
Muffin tin count: put up to five large pom-poms in the cups (an adult at the table).

note.mistake: Children guess the jam jars and muffins because they sit close together, saying "five" for any long row; others trace the 1 as a dot or a circle.
note.words: Say, "Touch each muffin and count with me." Ask, "How many blueberries? Two." Say, "One is a straight line down from the top."
note.watch: The page has five rows (one strip of bacon, two blueberries, three croissants, four jam jars and five muffins), each with a number to look at and two to trace. Watch touch counting, and that the last number said is the one traced.

lessons.check: Counts up to 5 foods and traces the matching number

lessons.title: Healthy Eating: Everyday and Sometimes Foods
lessons.objective: Children sort foods into everyday foods that help us grow and sometimes foods.
lessons.routine: Check for allergies first. Show real foods: broccoli, a tomato and an apple, with a cookie and a cupcake (or pictures of them). Talk about everyday foods that help our bodies grow strong and sometimes foods we eat at a party. Children taste soft-steamed broccoli and small tomato pieces (never whole cherry tomatoes), then build a "growing plate" with play food.
week: Food basket: broccoli, a tomato, an apple and a cookie; which help us grow every day?
Tasting (check for allergies first): soft-steamed broccoli and small tomato pieces; soft or juicy?
Healthy Foods page: lines from the cookie, the tomato, the cupcake and the broccoli to the boxes.
Growing plate: make a play-food lunch that is mostly everyday foods.
Grocery play: fill a basket with everyday foods and one sometimes food.

note.mistake: Children say sweet foods are "bad" and that one cookie makes you sick, or call fruit "not healthy" because it is sweet. Keep the words everyday and sometimes, not good and bad.
note.words: Say, "Broccoli is an everyday food. It helps us grow." Ask, "When do we eat cupcakes? On special days. It is a sometimes food." Say, "No food is bad. Some we eat every day, some sometimes."
note.watch: The page shows a cookie, a tomato, a cupcake and broccoli above a Healthy box and a Not Healthy box; read the boxes as everyday food and sometimes food. Watch that no child shames a food a friend likes.

lessons.check: Sorts two everyday foods and two sometimes foods

lessons.title: Healthy Eating Pencil Paths to Breakfast
lessons.objective: Children trace straight, zigzag, bumpy and wavy lines to breakfast foods.
lessons.routine: Pour and scoop at the sensory table: children pour sand from cup to cup with a funnel, scoop it with spoons and move play pancakes and fruit with tongs. Spread pretend butter (play-dough) on cardboard toast with a craft stick. Then draw lines with a finger in a tray of sand.
week: Pour and scoop: sand from cup to cup with a funnel and spoons.
Tongs practice: move play pancakes and fruit from plate to plate.
Finger lines in a tray of sand: straight, zigzag and wavy.
Pencil Path Practice: trace lines to the milk, the avocado, the cereal and the juice.
Spread pretend butter on cardboard toast with a craft stick.

note.mistake: Children trace fast and skip the middle of each line, jumping from the dot to the food, or hold the crayon in a fist like a spoon.
note.words: Say, "Hold your crayon with three fingers, not like a spoon." Ask, "Which food is at the end of the zigzag?" Say, "Go slowly, all the way to the juice."
note.watch: The page has four lines (straight, a zigzag, bumps and waves) ending at a bottle of milk, half an avocado, a bowl of cereal and a glass of juice. Look at the grip: three fingers, not a fist.

lessons.check: Holds the crayon with three fingers and traces a line to its end

themes.name: Post Office
themes.why: Letters, stamps and packages: how a letter travels from our hands to a mailbox and to a friend.

lessons.title: Post Office Word Cards: Stamp, Package, Scale
lessons.objective: Children name post office things (stamp, package, scale, delivery) and tell how a letter gets to a friend.
lessons.routine: Open a post office in dramatic play with envelopes, stickers for stamps, a kitchen scale, small boxes to wrap and a mail bag, and build a class mailbox from a shoebox. Children draw a letter, put a stamp on it and mail it. Read aloud a picture book about a letter's trip. Walk to the nearest mailbox together to mail a real letter to each family.
week: Post office opens: build the class mailbox; envelopes, sticker stamps, a scale and a mail bag.
Post Office Word Cards: scale, stamp, delivery and package.
Write a letter (draw or scribble) to someone at home and put a stamp on it.
Mailbox walk: mail our letters at the nearest mailbox.
Package play: wrap, weigh and deliver; clap stamp (1), pack-age (2), de-liv-er-y (4).

note.mistake: Children think the mail carrier writes the letters and call every box a "present"; the scale is a new picture, and many call it a clock or a phone.
note.words: Say, "A stamp pays for the letter's trip." Ask, "What do we put on the scale? A package, to see how heavy it is." Say, "The mail carrier brings the letters to our homes."
note.watch: The page shows four big cards: a scale with a screen, a stamp with a lighthouse, a mail carrier holding a package (delivery) and a cardboard package. Watch who can tell the order: write, stamp, mail, deliver.

lessons.check: Names a stamp, a package and the mail carrier and tells how a letter travels

lessons.title: Post Office: Which Letter Is First?
lessons.objective: Children count places from the flag in rows of post office pictures and find first, next and last.
lessons.routine: Line up five envelopes on a shelf, each with a different sticker, and a paper flag at one end. A "mail carrier" picks up the letters in order, counting first, second, third. Then set up five toy houses in a row and children deliver a letter to "the third house" or "the last house."
week: Letter line: five envelopes in a row; pick them up in order from the flag.
Toy houses in a row: deliver a letter to the third house, then the fifth.
Mailbox line: children line up with their letters and say their places.
Ordinal Numbers page: the teacher reads each chip; children count from the flag and mark.
Who gets mail first, next and last at our pretend post office?

note.mistake: Children deliver to the house they like best instead of the one in the place named; on the page some count only the envelopes and skip the mailbox and truck pictures between them.
note.words: Say, "Count every picture from the flag, not only the letters." Ask, "Which house is third?" Read, "This chip says second with an X. Count two from the flag and make an X."
note.watch: The page has three rows of five post office pictures (envelopes, a mailbox, a mail truck, stamps, a package, a scale and a mail carrier) with a flag at the left and two chips under each row, each with a circle or an X.

lessons.check: Counts places from the front to find the third and the last

lessons.title: Post Office: Who Brings the Mail?
lessons.objective: Children match workers to the job they do for people: the mail carrier brings the mail and the barber cuts hair.
lessons.routine: Watch for the mail carrier at school or invite one to visit, and ask what they carry and where it goes. Act out jobs: one child is the mail carrier with a bag, another is a barber with a toy comb and a mirror (no real scissors near hair). Children say what each worker does for people.
week: Mail carrier watch: see the mail arrive at school or meet a mail carrier.
Job charades: act out a mail carrier, a barber and a baker; friends guess.
Who Makes It? Who Does It? page: lines from the mail carrier and the barber to their jobs.
Barbershop play with toy combs and mirrors (no real scissors).
Thank-you picture for our mail carrier, drawn together.

note.mistake: Children think the mail carrier owns the mailbox or makes the letters, and match the barber to the mailbox because he stands beside the barber pole; some call a haircut "a thing" the barber makes.
note.words: Say, "A mail carrier brings letters to our homes. That is a job that helps people." Ask, "What does a barber do?" Say, "Some workers make things, and some do things for us."
note.watch: The page shows a mail carrier with a bag and a barber with scissors beside a barber pole on the left, and a child in a barber chair and a blue mailbox on the right; the child draws a line from each worker to the job that worker does.

lessons.check: Says what a mail carrier and a barber do for people

titles.maze-puzzles-k405-18: Picture Maze: Help the Mail Carrier Reach the Mailbox

lessons.title: Post Office Maze: Help the Mail Carrier
lessons.objective: Children follow a winding road with a crayon to help the mail carrier reach the mailbox.
lessons.routine: Set up a mail route in the room: tape roads between chairs, each chair with a child's name. Mail carriers walk the route with a bag and drop a letter at each chair. Then children post letters through slots of different sizes cut in a box (the teacher cuts the slots).
week: Mail route: walk the tape roads between chairs and drop a letter at each one.
Mail slots: push letters through slots of different sizes in a box.
Big paper map: drive a toy mail truck from the post office to a house.
Picture Maze: draw a line along the road from the mail carrier to the mailbox.
Draw a road from your house to a friend's house and deliver a letter on it.

note.mistake: Children choose the road that points straight at the mailbox and hit dead ends near the top; others draw through the grass between roads because the roads sit close together.
note.words: Say, "The mail carrier stays on the road." Ask, "This road stops. What can you do?" Say, "Go back to where the roads split and try the other way."
note.watch: The maze shows a winding tan road with many branches through the grass, the mail carrier at the left start, a blue mailbox with a flag at the top right, and a frog, a duck, an umbrella and a rain boot beside the road.

lessons.check: Finds the road to the goal and goes back at a dead end

themes.name: Friendship and Valentine's Day
themes.why: Being a good friend: taking turns, sharing, kind words, and making cards for the people we care about.

lessons.title: Friendship and Valentine's Day Word Cards
lessons.objective: Children name Valentine pictures (a heart key, candy, heart balloons, a cupcake) and say one kind thing to a friend.
lessons.routine: Use the class mailbox from Post Office week. Each child makes one card for every child in the class (with a name list and stickers), so no one is left out. Read aloud a picture book about friendship. At circle, pass a paper heart and say one kind thing to the friend next to you. Look at the card pictures together and decorate the mailbox with them.
week: Kind words circle: pass a paper heart and say one kind thing to a friend.
Valentine Word Cards: name the key, the candy, the balloons and the cupcake, then color.
Card making: one card for every friend, with stickers and drawings.
Mailbox: deliver a card to every friend's cubby, clapping the friend's name as we say it.
Friendship talk: what does a good friend do? Each child gives one idea.

note.mistake: Children think Valentine's cards are only for best friends and leave others out; the heart key and the heart balloons are new pictures, and many call the wrapped candy "a bow."
note.words: Say, "We make a card for every friend, so everyone feels loved." Ask, "What is this? It is a key with a heart." Model, "You are a good friend because you share."
note.watch: The page shows four big black-and-white cards to color: a key with a heart, a wrapped candy with hearts, heart balloons and a cupcake with a heart. Listen for a kind sentence when the child gives a card.

lessons.check: Says one kind thing to a friend and names the Valentine cards

lessons.title: Friendship and Valentine's: Places in Line
lessons.objective: Children find first, next and last and count places from the flag in rows of Valentine pictures.
lessons.routine: Five children line up at the class mailbox to deliver cards, with a paper flag at the front. Ask, "Who is first? Who is next? Who is last?" and count places together. Then line up five Valentine things on a table (a card, a paper heart, a cupcake picture, a candy box, a flower) and play "What is in third place?"
week: Mailbox line: five children line up to deliver; who is first, next and last?
Count places from the flag: first, second, third, fourth, fifth.
Valentine line: five things in a row; find the second and the fourth.
Ordinal Numbers page: the teacher reads each chip; children count from the flag and mark.
Line up for a friendship walk and say your place.

note.mistake: Children count the flag as first, or count the small hearts inside one picture instead of the pictures; with two chips under a row, many mark only one of them.
note.words: Say, "Start next to the flag. That picture is first." Ask, "Which is fourth? Count with me." If asked about the rings, say, "Grown-ups who love each other sometimes wear rings."
note.watch: The page has three rows of five black-and-white Valentine pictures (an envelope, a heart with wings, a pair of rings, a cake, heart balloons, a key, a lock) with a flag at the left and two chips under each row. Read both chips aloud for every row.

lessons.check: Finds first, next and last in a line and names the third

lessons.title: Friendship: Taking Turns and Sharing
lessons.objective: Children tell kind acts (sharing, taking turns, helping) from unkind ones and practice them.
lessons.routine: Play turn-taking games with a sand timer and one special toy: each child holds it until the sand runs out, then passes it on. Act out a puppet show: one puppet grabs the crayons, and the children show the puppet how to ask and share. All week, catch kind acts and add them to a friendship chart.
week: Puppet show: one puppet grabs the crayons; children teach it to ask and share.
Sand-timer turns with one special toy; pass it on when the sand runs out.
Taking Turns and Sharing page: circle the friends who are kind; cross out the others.
Helping hands: practice helping a friend who falls or drops their things.
Friendship chart: name the kind acts we saw this week.

note.mistake: Children cross out the slide because only one child is playing, but waiting for a turn is kind; some think sharing means giving a toy away forever, so they refuse. Others circle the torn drawing because the boy holding it smiles.
note.words: Ask, "Is this friend being kind? How can you tell?" Say, "Sharing means you use it now and get it back later." Ask, "How does the friend feel about the torn picture? What could he do to help?"
note.watch: The page shows four pictures: a child holding a friend's torn drawing while the friend cries, a child waiting by the slide while a friend slides, two children passing blocks across a table, and a child helping up a friend who fell. Three are kind; the torn drawing is not. Ask why each time.

lessons.check: Takes turns with a toy and names one kind act

lessons.title: Valentine Pencil Paths: Hearts, Slants and Crosses
lessons.objective: Children trace pencil paths and draw down lines, slants and crosses toward Valentine pictures.
lessons.routine: Make hearts with two hands and draw big hearts in the air. Lace yarn through holes punched around a cardboard heart. At the art table, children squeeze glue in down lines and crosses on paper and sprinkle paper hearts on top (an adult helps with the glue bottle).
week: Air hearts: draw big hearts in the air with a finger, then on a whiteboard.
Lacing hearts: lace yarn through the holes punched in a cardboard heart.
Pencil Path Practice: trace lines to the rings, the candy, the lock and the winged heart.
Glue lines: squeeze glue in down lines and crosses, then sprinkle paper hearts.
Down Lines, Slants and Crosses: trace each row to the bag, glasses, cake, calendar and flower.

note.mistake: On the slants children start at the bottom instead of the top dot, and crosses come out with one line much longer than the other; when lacing, they wrap the yarn around the edge instead of going through the holes.
note.words: Say, "Slants slide down, like a slide at the park." Ask, "Where is the top dot? Start there." Say, "Make the cross lines meet in the middle, like a hug."
note.watch: The pencil path page ends its four lines at a pair of rings, a candy, a lock and a heart with wings; the second page has rows of down lines, crosses, slants both ways and X crosses ending at a bag, glasses, a cake, a calendar and a flower.

lessons.check: Draws a slant and a cross, starting each line at the top

themes.name: Doctors and Healthy Habits
themes.why: Visiting the doctor and the dentist, and the habits that keep us healthy: brushing teeth, washing hands, sleep.

lessons.title: Doctors and Healthy Habits Word Cards
lessons.objective: Children name doctor's office things (doctor, tissue, wheelchair, crutches) and tell how each one helps.
lessons.routine: Set up a doctor's office with a toy stethoscope, bandages, a tissue box and a scale. Children take turns as doctor and patient, listen for heartbeats and wrap a "hurt" arm. Read aloud a picture book about a visit to the doctor or the dentist. Invite the school nurse to show a real stethoscope, and talk about how crutches and wheelchairs help people move.
week: Doctor's office opens: a toy stethoscope, bandages, tissues and a scale.
Doctor Word Cards: doctor, tissue, wheelchair and crutches; how does each one help?
School nurse visit: listen to a real heartbeat with the nurse's stethoscope.
Play doctor and patient with the card words; doctor and dentist start the same: /d/, /d/!
Tissue habit: catch a pretend sneeze in a tissue and throw it away.

note.mistake: Children say the doctor "gives shots" and is scary, or think a wheelchair or crutches mean someone is sick forever; the tissue box has a red cross on it, so many call it a first-aid kit.
note.words: Say, "A doctor helps us stay healthy and get better." Ask, "What do crutches do? They help someone walk while a leg heals." Say, "A wheelchair helps people move. Many people use one every day."
note.watch: The page shows four big cards: a doctor with a stethoscope, a tissue box, a wheelchair and a pair of crutches. Listen for what each one helps with, and for kind words about people who use wheelchairs.

lessons.check: Names four doctor's office things and says how one helps

lessons.title: Doctors' Tools in a Row: First and Last
lessons.objective: Children count places from the flag in rows of doctor's office pictures and mark the place each chip names.
lessons.routine: Line up five toy doctor things on a tray with a paper flag: a stethoscope, a box of bandages, a tissue box, a toy thermometer and a face mask. Children count places from the flag. Then patients wait in line at the pretend doctor's office and the nurse calls, "First patient, please," then the next, until the last.
week: Doctor's tray: five toy doctor things in a row; count places from the flag.
Waiting room line: the nurse calls the first patient, then the next one.
Who is last? Change the line and say the new last patient.
Ordinal Numbers page: the teacher reads each chip; children count from the flag and mark.
Line up for hand washing and say your place in line.

note.mistake: Children mark the picture they know (the ambulance) instead of the one in the place on the chip, or count from the end of the row nearest their drawing hand.
note.words: Say, "First is right next to the flag." Ask, "Which picture is fourth?" Read, "This chip says fifth with an X. Find the fifth picture and cross it out."
note.watch: The page has three rows of five hospital pictures (a hospital bed, a stretcher, a chest X-ray, tissues, a nurse, a mask, a thermometer, an ambulance, gloves, crutches) with a flag at the left and two chips under each row.

lessons.check: Finds first and last and counts to a place in a row of five

lessons.title: Healthy Habits: Brushing, Washing and Sleeping
lessons.objective: Children match healthy habits to the things we use (toothbrush, soap, bed, comb) and put the hand-washing steps in order.
lessons.routine: Practice the habits for real. Put a little glitter on hands as pretend germs and watch soap and water wash it away. Wash hands at the sink with soap while singing the ABC song (about 20 seconds). Brush a toy's teeth up and down with a big toothbrush and comb a doll's hair. Each child takes home a toothbrushing chart.
week: Glitter germs: put glitter on hands and wash it off with soap and water.
Hand washing for real: wet, soap, scrub while singing the ABC song, rinse, dry.
Healthy Habits page: lines from each child to the toothbrush, the soap, the bed or the comb.
Big toothbrush: brush a toy's teeth up and down; talk about visiting the dentist.
Hand Washing Steps page: write or point to 1 to 5 to put the steps in order.

note.mistake: Children rinse before using soap or skip drying, and think hands are clean if they look clean; on the steps page they number the pictures left to right instead of by what happens first.
note.words: Say, "Soap first, then scrub, scrub, scrub." Ask, "What do we do after we rinse? We dry." Ask, "What does this child need to get ready for bed?"
note.watch: The habits page shows four children (one under the moon at bedtime, one brushing at the mouth, one with messy hair, one at the sink) above a toothbrush, soap, a bed and a comb. The steps page has five sink pictures to number: wet, soap, scrub, rinse, dry; wet and rinse look alike, and rinse has bubbles on the hands. Writing is a challenge for the 5s; 3s point.

lessons.check: Washes hands with soap in the right order and names three healthy habits

titles.picture-tracing-easy-k425-2: Trace and Color the Picture: Bath Time

lessons.title: Doctors and Healthy Habits: Pencil Paths and Bath Time
lessons.objective: Children trace straight, wavy and bumpy lines to doctor's office pictures and trace a bath time picture.
lessons.routine: Wrap a doll's arm with a strip of soft cloth, going round and round like a bandage. Blow soap bubbles outside and draw bubble circles in the air with a finger. At the water table, squeeze a bottle and watch the water make wavy lines.
week: Bandage wrap: wind a soft cloth strip round and round a doll's arm.
Pencil Path Practice: trace lines to the scrubs, the thermometer, the mask and the bandage.
Bubbles outside: blow bubbles and draw bubble circles in the air.
Wavy Lines and Curves: trace to the scrubs, the stretcher, the doctor and the wheelchair.
Bath Time page: trace the tub, the rubber duck and the bubbles, then color.

note.mistake: Children trace the small bumps as one long flat line, and the wavy line flattens out halfway across; on Bath Time the bubbles are small circles that children close too early or draw on top of each other.
note.words: Say, "Little bumps, one after another, like ripples in the tub." Ask, "Did your bubble close? Come back to where you started." Say, "Trace slowly around the duck's head."
note.watch: The first page ends its four lines at blue scrubs, a thermometer, a face mask and a bandaged arm; the wavy page has curves and small bumps ending at scrubs, a stretcher, a doctor and a wheelchair; Bath Time has a tub, a rubber duck and round bubbles.

lessons.check: Traces wavy and bumpy lines and closes a small circle

themes.name: Weather
themes.why: Sun, rain, wind and snow: what the sky does each day and what we wear and do for each kind of weather.

lessons.title: Weather Word Cards: Puddle, Stormy, Rainbow, Mittens
lessons.objective: Children name weather words (puddle, stormy, rainbow, mittens) and describe today's weather.
lessons.routine: Start each day with a weather helper who looks out the window, tells the class the weather and puts a picture on the weather chart. Read aloud a picture book about rain or snow. On a rainy day, put on rain boots and stomp in puddles; on a sunny day, spray a fine mist from a spray bottle in the sunny window and look for a rainbow. Act out a storm with drums for thunder.
week: Weather helper: look out the window and tell the class today's weather.
Weather Word Cards: puddle, stormy, rainbow and mittens; act out each one.
Puddle stomp in rain boots, or a spray-bottle rainbow in the sunny window.
Storm sounds: drums for thunder, then clap the card words: rain-bow, pud-dle, storm-y.
Weather report: each child says one sentence about today's weather, holding a card.

note.mistake: Children say "it's raining" on any cloudy day and call a thunderstorm just "rain"; "stormy" is a new word, and many think mittens are a kind of weather rather than something we wear in it.
note.words: Say, "Stormy means rain, wind and thunder all together." Ask, "What do we wear when it snows? Mittens!" Ask, "What do you see in the sky today?"
note.watch: The page shows four big cards: a puddle, a storm cloud with rain and lightning (stormy), a rainbow and a pair of blue mittens. Watch whether children use the words to tell today's weather.

lessons.check: Names four weather words and tells today's weather

lessons.title: Weather: First, Next, Last on the Weather Line
lessons.objective: Children count places from the flag in rows of weather pictures and find first, next and last.
lessons.routine: Keep a weather line on the wall: each day, clip that day's weather picture in the next place after the flag. At the end of the week, count back through it: "The first day was sunny, the second day was rainy." Then five children hold weather cards in a row and the class finds who is first and last.
week: Weather line: clip today's weather picture in the first place.
Clip the second day's weather; say which picture is first and which is second.
Five children hold weather cards in a row; find first, third and last.
Ordinal Numbers page: the teacher reads each chip; children count from the flag and mark.
Weather line review: what was the weather on the third day?

note.mistake: Children count the raindrops or clouds inside one picture instead of counting the pictures, or start counting at the umbrella because it is bright; with two chips under a row, many do only the first.
note.words: Say, "Count the boxes from the flag, one box at a time." Ask, "What weather is in the fourth box?" Read, "This chip says second with a circle. Circle the second picture."
note.watch: The page has three rows of five weather pictures (a scarf, sunglasses, clouds, a raincoat, a storm cloud, a sun, a rainbow, a snowflake, an umbrella, mittens) with a flag at the left and two chips under each row.

lessons.check: Finds the first, third and last picture in a row of five

titles.weather-symbols-easy-k690-7: Ready for the Weather: Rain and a Hot Day
titles.weather-symbols-easy-k690-8: Ready for the Weather: A Hot Day and a Snowstorm

lessons.title: Weather: Ready for Rain, Snow and Sun
lessons.objective: Children choose what to wear or bring for rain, a hot day and a snowstorm.
lessons.routine: Keep a "ready bag" by the door with an umbrella, sunglasses, a closed tube of sunscreen to look at, mittens, a water bottle and a wool hat. Each morning, look outside and pick what we need. Test a raincoat: spray water on a raincoat and on a cotton shirt and see which one stays dry.
week: Ready bag: look outside and pick what we need from the bag.
Raincoat test: spray water on a raincoat and a cotton shirt; which stays dry?
Ready for the Weather page: circle what to bring for rain and for a hot day.
Dress the bear: put the right clothes on a teddy bear for snow, rain and sun.
Second Ready for the Weather page: a hot day and a snowstorm.

note.mistake: Children circle what they like (sunglasses in the rain) or what they wore that day; the sunscreen tube is new to many, and some pick mittens for a hot day "just in case."
note.words: Ask, "Will sunglasses help in the rain?" Say, "In a snowstorm we need a warm coat." Ask, "What keeps us cool on a hot day? A drink of water."
note.watch: The first page has a rain row (an umbrella, sunglasses, sunscreen) and a hot row (mittens, a water bottle, a wool hat); the second a hot row (a water bottle, a coat, mittens) and a snowstorm row (flip-flops, shorts, a pink coat). The child circles the right thing in each row.

lessons.check: Chooses what to wear for rain, snow and a hot day and says why

titles.picture-tracing-easy-k424-6: Spirals and Loops to Trace: The Windy Day

lessons.title: Weather Tracing: A Rainy Day and a Windy Day
lessons.objective: Children trace raindrops, an umbrella and a cloud, then spirals and loops for a windy day.
lessons.routine: Make it rain: children tap their fingertips on the table for light rain, then harder, and paint raindrops at the easel. On a windy day, take streamers outside and watch them twirl, then twirl our arms the same way. Make a paper kite with a long tail and draw loops along the tail.
week: Rain fingers: tap the table softly, then harder; paint raindrops at the easel.
A Rainy Day page: trace the cloud, the drops, the umbrella, the duck and the boot.
Streamer walk outside: watch the wind twirl them and twirl our arms the same way.
The Windy Day page: trace the kite, its loopy tail, the spiral and the balloon string.
Make a paper kite and draw loops along its tail.

note.mistake: Children make raindrops as dots instead of drops with a point on top, and the kite's tail loops grow bigger and bigger until they run off the page; spirals turn into circles stacked on each other.
note.words: Say, "A raindrop has a point at the top and a round bottom." Ask, "Can you make the loops the same size, like the kite's tail?" Say, "Spiral in, round and round, smaller and smaller."
note.watch: The rainy day page shows a cloud, four drops, an umbrella, a duck and a rain boot; the windy day page has a kite with a loopy tail, a spiral blown by the wind and a balloon on a string. Look for drops with a point and loops of even size.

lessons.check: Traces raindrops and a kite's loops along the dashes

themes.name: Transportation
themes.why: Things that go on land and water (week 1) and things that fly (week 2): how people and things travel.

lessons.title: Transportation: Sort Boats, Bikes and Motorcycles
lessons.objective: Children cut out vehicle pictures, sort them into groups of the same kind and tell how each one moves.
lessons.routine: Tip a bin of toy vehicles onto the rug: boats, bikes, motorcycles, cars, trains and planes. Children sort them by kind into hoops, then by where they go (road, water, sky). Read aloud a picture book about things that go. Before the pages, children practice cutting along straight lines on paper strips with child-safe scissors.
week: Vehicle bin: name each toy vehicle and how it moves.
Sort the toy vehicles by kind into hoops and say the rule for each hoop.
Snip practice: cut along straight lines on paper strips with child-safe scissors.
Cut, Sort and Paste page: cut the bikes, ships and sailboats and glue each in its column.
Vehicle parade: each child holds a toy vehicle and says its name and what it does.
Sort again: things that fly, things that float and things that roll; say the rule for each hoop.
Cut and Paste: Two Big Groups page: cut the ships and motorcycles apart.
Glue the ships in one group and the motorcycles in the other.
Tell a friend why this ship goes here: it floats on water.
Vehicle wall: put up the sorted pages and name every vehicle on them.

note.mistake: Children glue the sailboat with the bikes because both are red, or put a ship with the motorcycles because they were next to each other on the strip; many cut right through the middle of a picture.
note.words: Ask, "What is the picture at the top of this column? Find all the ones like it." Say, "A sailboat has a sail. A ship is a big boat with no sail." Ask, "Does it have wheels? Does it float?"
note.watch: The first page has three columns topped by a ship, a sailboat and a bike, with six pictures to cut at the bottom; the second has two big groups, a ship and a motorcycle, with eight pictures in two strips to cut. Help 3s cut; watch the sorting.

lessons.check: Sorts vehicles by kind and says the rule for each group

lessons.title: Transportation: The Tallest and the Biggest
lessons.objective: Children compare vehicles, find the tallest in a row and circle every big one.
lessons.routine: Stand toy sailboats and rockets on the table and find the tallest by lining up their bottoms. Fold a big paper plane and a small one (the teacher folds) and fly them outside. Stand beside a tall cardboard rocket taped to the wall and see who is shorter and who is taller than its window.
week: Toy boats and rockets on the table: line up the bottoms and find the tallest.
Tall and short walk: find tall and short things on the playground.
Tall and Short page: circle the tallest sailboat or rocket in each row.
Paper planes: a big one and a small one (the teacher folds); fly them.
Stand beside the cardboard rocket on the wall: who reaches its window?
Big and small sort: big vehicles and small vehicles from the toy bin.
Big Ones Only page: circle every big plane and leave the small ones.
Garage game: big trucks park in the big garage, small cars in the small one.
Draw a big boat and a small boat and tell which one is bigger.
Show a friend the tallest and the biggest vehicle you can find in the room.

note.mistake: Children pick the tallest by the flag on top of the sail; on Big Ones Only they circle the three big planes in the top row and stop, missing the big plane at the bottom right.
note.words: Ask, "Which sailboat is the tallest? Line up the bottoms." Say, "Tall means from the bottom to the top." Ask, "Are there more big planes? Look in every row."
note.watch: The Tall and Short page has three rows of four (sailboats, rockets, sailboats), and the child circles the tallest in each; the Big Ones Only page has nine purple planes, four big and five small, and the child circles every big one.

lessons.check: Finds the tallest in a row and circles every big one

lessons.title: Transportation: Land, Water and Air
lessons.objective: Children sort vehicles by where they travel (land, water, air) and things that can fly and cannot fly.
lessons.routine: Make three zones on the rug: a road (black paper), water (a tub of water) and air (a string across the room). Children test toy vehicles: does it float? Boats go in the tub, cars on the road, paper planes hang on the string. Then test what flies: drop a feather, a paper plane and a block from the same height.
week: Three zones: road, water tub and air string; put each toy vehicle where it travels.
Float test: which toy vehicles float in the water tub?
Land, Water and Air page: lines from the six vehicles to land, water or air.
Vehicle watch: count cars passing the school, look for a plane in the sky.
Sing "Row, Row, Row Your Boat" and act out other vehicles.
Fly test: drop a feather, a paper plane and a block; which ones glide?
Things That Fly page: lines from the owl, the bee, the fish and the car to can fly or cannot.
Paper planes: fold and fly them; talk about wings.
Look outside for things that fly: birds, bugs, leaves in the wind.
Sort toy vehicles and toy animals into can fly and cannot fly.

note.mistake: Children put the helicopter on land because it sits on legs, and say a fish flies because it "swims up"; many think every animal can fly if it jumps high enough.
note.words: Ask, "Where does a ship go? On the water." Say, "A helicopter flies in the air." Ask, "Can a bee fly? Can a car?"
note.watch: The first page shows six vehicles (a plane, a truck, a boat, a helicopter, a train and a ship) and three boxes, Land, Water and Air; the second shows an owl, a bee, a goldfish and a car above Can Fly and Cannot Fly.

lessons.check: Sorts vehicles into land, water and air and says which things can fly

titles.picture-tracing-easy-k420-5: Look, Then Trace: Balloon and Helicopter

lessons.title: Transportation Tracing: Bus, Balloon and Helicopter
lessons.objective: Children trace pencil paths to vehicles, a bus made of shapes, and a hot air balloon and a helicopter.
lessons.routine: Roll toy cars through paint on big paper to make wheel tracks. Glue a paper bus from shapes: a long rectangle, square windows and circle wheels. Outside, walk a "bus route" along chalk lines and stop at each "bus stop." Hold a paper-plate steering wheel and turn it along a tape road.
week: Car tracks: roll toy cars through paint on big paper.
Chalk bus route: walk the lines and stop at each bus stop.
Pencil Path Practice: trace to the ship, the motorcycle, the digger and the plane.
Paper shape bus: glue a long rectangle, square windows and circle wheels.
The Shape Bus page: trace the rectangle, the squares and the circles, then color the circles.
Steering wheel drive: turn a paper-plate wheel along a tape road.
Look, Then Trace page: trace the hot air balloon and the helicopter next to each picture.
Paper helicopter (the teacher folds): drop it and watch it spin down.
Draw a road for a car, a sky path for a plane and a wavy path for a boat.
Trace and color a vehicle of your choice from this week's pages.

note.mistake: Children trace the bus wheels as ovals that do not close, and on the hot air balloon they trace the outside and skip the stripes; the helicopter's thin rotor lines get missed.
note.words: Say, "Circle wheels: go round and close them." Ask, "Did you trace the stripes inside the balloon?" Say, "Look at the picture first, then trace the same picture next to it."
note.watch: The pencil path page ends at a ship, a motorcycle, a digger and a plane; the shape bus has a long rectangle, square windows, circle wheels and extra shapes; Look, Then Trace shows a hot air balloon and a helicopter in frames with a dashed copy beside each.

lessons.check: Traces the shapes of a bus and a balloon and closes the circles

themes.name: Plants and Gardens
themes.why: Planting seeds in spring: what a plant needs to grow, flowers and vegetables in the garden.

titles.picture-word-cards-easy-flowers-k324-45: Flower Word Cards: Phlox, Crocus, Peony, Dahlia
titles.picture-word-cards-vegetables-k324-186: Vegetable Word Cards: Lettuce, Squash, Tomato, Radish

lessons.title: Plants and Gardens Word Cards: Flowers and Vegetables
lessons.objective: Children name flowers and vegetables (crocus, dahlia, tomato, radish, pumpkin, lettuce and more) and tell which part we look at or eat.
lessons.routine: Bring a pot of real flowers and a basket of real vegetables (a tomato, a radish, lettuce, celery). Children smell the flowers and wash the vegetables in a tub. Read aloud a picture book about a garden. Plant marigold seeds in cups with an adult at the table (seeds are small). Name each card picture first: crocus, peony, dahlia and phlox are new words.
week: Garden basket: wash the real tomato, radish, lettuce and celery in a tub.
Flower Word Cards: phlox, crocus, peony and dahlia; name the pictures first.
Plant marigold seeds in cups (an adult at the table) and label each cup.
Vegetable Word Cards: where does each grow? Clap squash (1), pump-kin (2), to-ma-to (3).
Garden walk: look for flowers and vegetables at school or in a neighbor's garden.

note.mistake: The flower names phlox, crocus, peony and dahlia are new: let children say "flower" while they learn them. On the vegetable cards the yellow squash looks like a pear and the cauliflower gets called "white broccoli"; name those pictures first.
