note.words: Say, "This flower is a dahlia. Let's say it together: DAH-lee-uh." Ask, "Which vegetable grows under the ground? The radish." Say, "This yellow squash looks like a pear, but it is a vegetable."
note.watch: The flower cards show a phlox, a crocus, a peony and a dahlia; the vegetable page has eight smaller cards: lettuce, a squash, a cauliflower, a tomato, asparagus, a radish, a pumpkin and celery. Watch for "flower" and "vegetable" used correctly even before the new names stick.

lessons.check: Names two flowers and four vegetables and says where one grows

lessons.title: Plants and Gardens: Flowers in a Row
lessons.objective: Children count places from the flag in rows of flowers and find first, next and last.
lessons.routine: Set five paper flowers in a row on the window sill with a flag at one end and name the first and the last. Children are seeds in a row on the rug: the first seed grows up, then the next, until the last. Line up the class seed cups and water the second cup, then the fourth.
week: Paper flower row on the window sill with a flag: name the first and the last.
Grow game: children are seeds in a row; the first grows up, then the next.
Watering line: water the second and the fourth seed cup in the row.
Ordinal Numbers page: the teacher reads each chip; children count from the flag and mark.
Sprout check: which cup in the row sprouted first?

note.mistake: Children count the petals of one flower instead of the flowers, or count the flag; the flowers look alike, so many lose their place in the middle of the row.
note.words: Say, "Count the flowers, not the petals." Ask, "Which flower is fifth?" Say, "Keep your finger on the flower you are counting."
note.watch: The page has three rows of five flowers (red flowers, a sunflower, tulips, a blue flower, a lily, a purple spike) with a flag at the left and two chips under each row, each with a circle or an X. Read each chip aloud.

lessons.check: Counts places from the flag to find the first, third and last flower

lessons.title: Plants and Gardens: What Plants Need to Grow
lessons.objective: Children find out that a plant needs water and light to grow and circle the plant that gets both.
lessons.routine: The week before, sprout bean seeds on a wet paper towel in a zip bag. On the first day, plant two sprouted beans in cups the same way, with an adult at the table. Put one cup in a sunny window and one in a dark closet, and water both. Each day children look and draw what they see. By the end of the week the plant in the light is green and strong; the one in the dark is pale yellow and floppy, even if it grew taller.
week: Plant two beans that sprouted on a wet paper towel last week (an adult at the table).
One cup in the sunny window, one in a dark closet; water both and guess what will happen.
What Plants Need page: circle the plant that gets both water and sun.
Check the cups: look at the color of the leaves and stems and draw what we see.
Compare the cups: the plant in the light is green and strong; the one in the dark is pale and weak.

note.mistake: Children think plants eat soil or need toys and music to grow, and on the page they circle the plant with a drum or a book because that picture is fun; many think the tallest plant is the healthiest, but the plant in the dark grows tall, pale and floppy.
note.words: Ask, "What does our plant need: water, light, or a toy?" Say, "Plants need water and light to grow green and strong." Ask, "Which plant is green? Which one is pale? Why?"
note.watch: The page has five rows, each with two potted plants and arrows from what each one gets (a sun, a water drop, blocks, a glove, a drum, a book, a guitar, a pencil); the child circles the plant that gets both water and sun.

lessons.check: Says a plant needs water and light and shows it with our seed cups

titles.picture-tracing-easy-k425-4: Trace and Color the Picture: The Flowerpot

lessons.title: Plants and Gardens: Trace the Flowerpot
lessons.objective: Children trace a flowerpot picture and pencil paths to flowers.
lessons.routine: Plant a real flower in a pot together and press the soil down with our fingers. Make tissue-paper flowers: crumple the petals and twist the stems. Draw flowers in the sand tray with a stick: a circle in the middle and petals around it.
week: Plant a real flower in a pot and press the soil with our fingers.
Tissue-paper flowers: crumple the petals and twist the stems.
The Flowerpot page: trace the window, the butterfly, the flower in its pot and the teacup.
Sand-tray flowers: draw a circle and petals with a stick.
Pencil Path Practice: trace lines to the clover and the flowers.

note.mistake: Children trace the flower as one big circle and miss each petal's curve, and skip the lines that cross the window; on the pencil paths they stop at the flower before the line ends.
note.words: Say, "Trace each petal, one at a time." Ask, "What is in the window? What is on the table?" Say, "Go all the way to the clover."
note.watch: The Flowerpot page shows a window with four panes, a butterfly, a flower in a pot, a teacup with steam and a table line; the pencil path page ends its four lines at a clover and three flowers. Look at each petal traced.

lessons.check: Traces a flower petal by petal and a window with its lines

themes.name: Bugs
themes.why: Bugs in the grass and the garden: ants, ladybugs, bees, caterpillars and worms, and the homes they build.

lessons.title: Bugs Word Cards: Ant, Slug, Centipede, Millipede
lessons.objective: Children name small creatures (ant, slug, centipede, millipede) and say how each one moves.
lessons.routine: Go on a bug walk with plastic magnifying glasses. An adult lifts a log or a flat rock, the class looks without touching, and the adult puts it back gently. Watch how each creature moves and count legs from a distance. Read aloud a picture book about bugs. Back inside, match the bugs we saw to photos and make finger legs walk across the table.
week: Bug walk: look under a log with magnifying glasses; look, don't touch.
Bugs Word Cards: the centipede, millipede, slug and ant; name the pictures first.
Move like a bug: march like an ant, slide like a slug, wiggle many legs like a centipede.
Bug photo table: match each card to a photo; clap ant (1), slug (1), cen-ti-pede (3).
Bug report: each child tells a friend one bug they saw and how it moved.

note.mistake: Children call every small creature a "bug" or an "ant"; centipede and millipede are new words that look alike (both have many legs), and the slug gets called a snail with no shell. Name the pictures first, then the differences.
note.words: Say, "A slug is like a snail with no shell." Ask, "Does a centipede have many legs or a few?" Say, "We look at bugs with our eyes, not our hands."
note.watch: The page shows four big cards (a centipede, a millipede, a slug and an ant), each with its word. Listen for "centipede" and "millipede" after you name them, and for "look, don't touch" on the walk.

lessons.check: Names four small creatures and how one of them moves

lessons.title: Bugs: Count and Trace 6 to 10
lessons.objective: Children count groups of 6 to 10 bugs, with help, and trace the number that tells how many.
lessons.routine: Fill a garden tray with paper bugs. Children count them onto a ten-frame, one bug in each box, so they can see how many: six butterflies, then seven bees. Count the dots on paper ladybugs. Act out a counting rhyme with fingers crawling up the arm like bugs, from one to ten.
week: Bug tray: count paper bugs onto a ten-frame, one in each box.
How many bugs? Fill the ten-frame to 6, then 7, and count the empty boxes.
Ladybug dots: count 6 to 10 dots on paper ladybugs.
Count and Trace page: count each row of bugs and trace the number (a challenge for the 5s).
Bug hunt: find paper bugs hidden in the room and count them up to ten.

note.mistake: With 6 to 10 bugs in two rows, children lose count where one row ends and the next begins and count a bug twice; 6 and 9 get traced upside down.
note.words: Say, "Touch each bee and push it a little as you count." Ask, "Where did we stop? Keep going from there." Say, "This is a big number for us. Let's count slowly together."
note.watch: The page has five rows (six butterflies, seven bees, eight red worms, nine ladybugs and ten green caterpillars), each with a number to look at and two to trace. It is a challenge for the 5s: 3s and young 4s count with the teacher and trace one number only.

lessons.check: Counts 6 to 10 bugs, touching each one, with help

lessons.title: Bugs and Their Homes
lessons.objective: Children match animals to their homes: the ant to an anthill, the spider to a web, the bee to a hive, and more.
lessons.routine: Look for bug homes on the playground: an anthill, a spider web on a fence (look closely, don't touch) and holes chewed in leaves. Back inside, build bug homes: a yarn web across a chair, a hive from an egg carton and a sand anthill. Children put toy bugs in the homes and say who lives there.
week: Bug home hunt outside: an anthill, a spider web and chewed leaves (look, don't touch).
Build homes: a yarn web, an egg-carton hive and a sand anthill.
Animal Homes page: draw a line from each animal to its home.
Toy bugs go home: put each toy bug in the home it built.
Draw a bug in its home and tell a friend about it.

note.mistake: Children match the bee to a flower (where it visits) instead of the hive, and the rabbit to the anthill because both are holes in the ground; some think spiders live only in houses.
note.words: Ask, "Where does a bee live? In a hive." Say, "A spider makes its own home: a web." Ask, "Who lives in a hole under the ground?"
note.watch: The page shows six animals on the left (an ant, a rabbit, a spider, a bee, a bird and a beaver) and six homes on the right (a web, an anthill, a nest, a burrow, a hive and a dam). The bugs are the ant, the spider and the bee; the others are part of the same page.

lessons.check: Matches an ant, a spider and a bee to their homes

titles.maze-puzzles-easy-k406-3: My First Maze: Help the Ladybug Get to the Sunflower
titles.maze-puzzles-k413-10: Maze Coloring Page: The Bee and the Flower

lessons.title: Bugs Mazes: The Ladybug and the Bee
lessons.objective: Children follow a maze road to help a ladybug reach a sunflower and a bee reach a flower, then color the garden.
lessons.routine: Build a block maze on the floor and children crawl through it like ladybugs to a paper sunflower. Fly a toy bee on a stick along a ribbon path laid on the table without leaving the ribbon. Draw finger roads through a tray of soil from a toy bug to a flower.
week: Block maze: crawl like ladybugs to the paper sunflower.
Bee flight: move a toy bee along a ribbon path without leaving it.
My First Maze page: help the ladybug get to the sunflower.
Soil tray: draw finger roads from a toy bug to a flower.
Maze Coloring Page: draw the bee's way to the flower, then color the garden.

note.mistake: On the coloring maze children color the garden before they find the road and lose the path, and the road's edges are thin black lines that the crayon wanders across; on the ladybug maze they go straight up the middle of the grass.
note.words: Say, "Find the road first, color later." Ask, "Where does the bee start? At the A." Say, "Stay between the black lines."
note.watch: The ladybug maze has a wide road from the ladybug at the bottom left to a sunflower at the top right, with one dead end and a bee, a caterpillar and flowers in the grass; the coloring maze is a black-and-white garden with the bee at the start (A), a winding road with dead ends to a flower at the top right, and a butterfly, a bird, a plant and a sun to color.

lessons.check: Finds the road through a maze and stays between its edges

themes.name: Spring
themes.why: Spring babies and birds: chicks, lambs and calves with their mothers (week 1), then birds, eggs and nests (week 2).

titles.picture-word-cards-easy-spring-k324-78: Spring Word Cards: Grass, Chick, Lamb, Caterpillar
titles.picture-word-cards-easy-birds-k324-22: Bird Word Cards: Pelican, Flamingo, Hornbill, Toucan
titles.picture-word-cards-easy-birds-2-k324-23: Bird Word Cards: Macaw, Toucan, Penguin, Hawk

lessons.title: Spring Word Cards: Baby Animals and Birds
lessons.objective: Children name spring baby animals and birds (chick, lamb, caterpillar, flamingo, toucan, penguin, hawk and more) and say one thing each does.
lessons.routine: Bring spring in: a photo of a nest or a nest the class builds from twigs and yarn, hard-boiled eggs to look at, and photos of lambs, chicks and calves. Read aloud a picture book about baby animals. Go on a bird walk with paper-tube binoculars and hang a feeder made from an orange half and birdseed (the adult cuts). Talk about who hatches from an egg.
week: Spring table: look at a nest photo, eggs and photos of lambs, chicks and calves.
Spring Word Cards: grass, chick, lamb and caterpillar; who will each one grow into?
Peep like a chick, hop like a lamb, crawl like a caterpillar; clap chick (1), cat-er-pil-lar (4).
Hatch game: children curl up like eggs and hatch as chicks.
Who comes from an egg? Sort the spring cards into egg and not egg.
Bird walk with paper binoculars: look and listen for birds.
Bird Word Cards: pelican, flamingo, hornbill and toucan; name the pictures first.
Hang an orange-half bird feeder (the adult cuts) and watch who comes.
Bird Word Cards: macaw, toucan, penguin and hawk; which ones can fly?
Spring report: each child names a bird or a baby animal and what it does.

note.mistake: Children call every bird "birdie" and mix up the toucan and the hornbill; pelican, hornbill and macaw are new words to name first. Many think the caterpillar is a worm and that lambs hatch from eggs like chicks.
note.words: Say, "A caterpillar hatches from a tiny egg and grows into a butterfly." Ask, "Does a lamb come from an egg? No, it is born from its mother." Say, "This is a toucan. Look at its big, colorful beak."
note.watch: The spring cards show grass, a chick, a lamb and a caterpillar; the first bird cards show a pelican, a flamingo, a hornbill and a toucan; the second a macaw, a toucan, a penguin and a hawk. Only the hawk lives near most schools: on the bird walk, listen for bird words (beak, wings, feathers, nest).

lessons.check: Names three baby animals and three birds

lessons.title: Spring: Dot-to-Dot Chick and Ostrich, 1 to 10
lessons.objective: Children count from 1 to 10 in order and connect the dots to finish a hatching chick and an ostrich.
lessons.routine: Fill an egg carton with ten paper eggs numbered 1 to 10, each hiding a paper chick. Children open the eggs in order, counting aloud. Then mix the eggs up on the rug and children put them back in the carton from 1 to 10. Hop like chicks along a 1-to-10 number path on the floor.
week: Egg carton count: open ten paper eggs numbered 1 to 10, in order.
Fix the eggs: put the mixed-up paper eggs back in order from 1 to 10.
Chick hops along a 1-to-10 path on the floor, saying each number.
Dot-to-Dot 1 to 10: connect the dots to finish the chick hatching from its egg.
Color the chick and count its toes and the pieces of shell.
Bird tracks: count bird footprints printed on paper, 1 to 10.
What comes next? The teacher says a number; children say the next one.
Dot-to-Dot 1 to 10: start at 1 under the ostrich's beak and join the dots down its long neck.
Ostrich and chick: which one has the longer neck? Count the dots on each.
Count the birds at our feeder, or in a picture, up to ten.

note.mistake: Children connect the chick's dots in a circle around its head because the numbers curve, and skip from 4 to 6; on the ostrich the dots run close together down a thin neck, and children lose the order where they bunch up.
note.words: Say, "Say the number, find it, then draw." Ask, "What comes after 5?" Say, "Start under the ostrich's beak and go down, down, down its long neck to number 10."
note.watch: The chick page shows a chick breaking out of a cracked egg, the top of its head made by dots 1 to 10 in a curve; on the ostrich page the head is drawn, and dots 1 to 10 run from under the beak down the front of the neck to the chest. Each page has a number strip at the bottom.

lessons.check: Joins dots 1 to 10 in order on two pictures

titles.science-match-k205-3: Animal Babies: Cow, Butterfly, Horse, Hen, Sheep
titles.science-match-k205-4: Animal Babies: Hen, Horse, Sheep, Cow, Butterfly

lessons.title: Spring: Animal Babies and Their Parents
lessons.objective: Children match grown-up animals to their babies (hen and chick, cow and calf, sheep and lamb, horse and foal, butterfly and caterpillar).
lessons.routine: Use photos of baby animals and toy animal families, big and small. Children match each baby toy to its parent and say the baby's name: chick, calf, lamb, foal. If you can, keep caterpillars in a class habitat and watch them change (look, don't touch). Talk about how babies look like their parents and how they look different.
week: Toy animal families: match each baby to its grown-up and say the baby's name.
Baby names: chick, calf, lamb, foal and caterpillar, each with its parent.
Animal Babies page: draw a line from each grown-up animal to its baby.
Alike and different: how is a lamb like a sheep? How is it different?
Caterpillar watch: a class habitat or photos; what will it become?
Baby photos: children bring a baby photo of themselves; how have we changed?
Second Animal Babies page: the hen, horse, sheep, cow and butterfly in a new order.
Act out a mother animal and its baby; friends guess which ones.
Draw an animal and its baby side by side.
Tell a friend which baby looks most like its parent and which looks different.

note.mistake: Children match by color or size (the white chick to the white sheep), and nearly everyone matches the caterpillar to the wrong parent because it looks nothing like a butterfly; some think a calf is a baby horse.
note.words: Ask, "Who is this baby's mother? Look at the shape, not the color." Say, "A caterpillar grows into a butterfly." Ask, "What is a baby cow called? A calf."
note.watch: The first page has a cow, a butterfly, a horse, a hen and a sheep on the left and a chick, a calf, a caterpillar, a lamb and a foal on the right; the second has the same animals in a new order. The child draws a line from each grown-up to its baby.

lessons.check: Matches five grown-up animals to their babies and names three babies

titles.maze-puzzles-easy-k408-2: Babies and Mothers Maze in the Meadow
titles.maze-puzzles-hard-k406-13: My First Maze: Help the Bird Get to the Birdhouse
titles.maze-puzzles-easy-k405-12: Picture Maze: Help the Swan Reach the Nest

lessons.title: Spring Mazes: Babies, Mothers and Nests
lessons.objective: Children draw a line along maze roads to help baby animals find their mothers and birds reach their nests.
lessons.routine: Lay tape roads on the floor: children carry a baby animal toy along a road to its matching mother toy. Build a nest from twigs, yarn and paper strips in a bowl. Outside, follow a chalk trail from a "baby bird" to a hoop nest, and turn back at the chalk dead ends.
week: Baby finds mother: carry a baby animal toy along a tape road to its mother.
Babies and Mothers Maze: draw a line from each baby to its own mother.
Chalk trail outside: walk from the baby bird to the hoop nest.
Nest building: weave twigs, yarn and paper strips in a bowl.
Maze talk: where did you have to turn back? Show a friend.
Ribbon path on the table: fly a paper bird along it to a paper nest.
My First Maze: help the bird get to the birdhouse.
Sand tray: draw a road for a toy duck to its nest.
Picture Maze: help the swan reach the nest along the winding road.
Draw your own maze from a bird to a nest for a friend to try.

note.mistake: On the babies and mothers maze children follow one road and then send all three babies to the mother they reached first; on the swan maze they start at the nest because it is at the top of the page.
note.words: Say, "Each baby has its own road to its own mother." Ask, "Which baby is number 2? Follow its road." Say, "The swan starts at the bottom. Find the arrow."
note.watch: The meadow maze has a chick, a calf and a lamb at the top, numbered 1 to 3, with roads down to a cow, a sheep and a hen; the birdhouse maze has a wide road with dead ends from a bird to a birdhouse in the sky; the swan maze has a winding road from the swan at the bottom right to a nest at the top left.

lessons.check: Follows a maze road from a baby to its mother and from a bird to its nest

themes.name: Frogs and the Pond
themes.why: Life at the pond: frogs, turtles, ducks and fish, and what a frog needs in its home.

lessons.title: Frogs and the Pond Word Cards
lessons.objective: Children name pond and reptile animals (frog, turtle, alligator, gecko) and tell where each one lives.
lessons.routine: Make a pond in the water table with toy frogs, turtles and an alligator, rocks and green paper lily pads. Children make each animal swim, rest on a rock or hide. Read aloud a picture book about a pond. Show a photo of a gecko climbing a wall. Sing a counting song about frogs on a log and move the toy frogs as the class sings.
week: Water-table pond: toy frogs, turtles and an alligator swim, rest on rocks and hide.
Pond Word Cards: alligator, frog, gecko and turtle; name the gecko first.
Frog jumps: one hop on a lily pad for each clap: frog (1), tur-tle (2), al-li-ga-tor (4).
Where does it live? Put each card by the water table or by the land rock.
Pond story: each child tells what one pond animal did today.

note.mistake: Children call the alligator a "dinosaur" or a "crocodile" and the gecko a "lizard" (right, and gecko is its name); some think a turtle can take its shell off.
note.words: Say, "A gecko is a kind of lizard that can climb walls." Ask, "Where does a frog like to sit? On a lily pad." Say, "A turtle's shell is part of its body. It cannot take it off."
note.watch: The page shows four big cards: an alligator, a frog, a gecko and a turtle. Name the gecko first, then watch who tells where each animal lives (in water, on land or both).

lessons.check: Names a frog, a turtle, an alligator and a gecko and where one lives

lessons.title: Frogs and the Pond: One More
lessons.objective: Children count a small group of pond animals, draw one more and say how many there are now.
lessons.routine: Put three toy frogs on a log and say, "One more frog jumps on. How many now?" Children count, add one frog and count again. Repeat with toy turtles and lizards, always adding just one. Then children take turns being the frog that jumps onto a mat, and the class says the new number.
week: Frogs on a log: three toy frogs; one more jumps on; count again.
One more turtle: add one turtle at a time and say the new number.
Be the frog: children jump onto a mat one at a time; the class says how many now.
One More page: count the pond animals, draw one more and say how many now.
One more block: build towers and add one block, saying the new number.

note.mistake: Many children start counting again from 1 after adding, which is fine, but some draw two or three more in the box or forget to count the one they drew; writing the new number is for the 5s.
note.words: Say, "Three frogs. One more jumps on. Count them all." Ask, "Is it more or fewer now?" Say, "Draw just one more frog in the box."
note.watch: The page has four rows (three frogs, two orange lizards, four turtles and one alligator), each with a "1 more" label, an empty box to draw one more and a box for the new number. Watch that only one is drawn and that all are counted.

lessons.check: Adds one more to a group of up to 5 and says the new number

lessons.title: Frogs and the Pond: A Home for a Frog
lessons.objective: Children find what a frog needs in its home (water, food, a place to hide) and build a frog home.
lessons.routine: Build a frog home in a clear tub: a little water, rocks, plants and a log, with a toy frog. Talk about what the frog needs: water to keep its skin wet, bugs to eat and a place to hide. Look at photos of eggs, tadpoles and frogs. Children check the home each day and add one thing a frog needs.
week: Frog home tub: water, rocks, plants and a log for a toy frog.
What does a frog need? Water, food and a place to hide.
Frog photos: egg, tadpole, frog; which comes first?
A Home for a Frog page: cut and glue the pond, the grasshopper and the grass, then draw the frog.
Tell a friend why the frog needs each thing in its home.

note.mistake: Children add things they like to the frog's home (a toy, a bed) and think frogs eat leaves; some glue the grasshopper in as the frog's pet rather than its food.
note.words: Ask, "What does a frog eat? Bugs, like a grasshopper." Say, "A frog needs water to keep its skin wet." Ask, "Where can the frog hide?"
note.watch: The page shows a frog in a box at the top, a big frame for the frog's home and three pictures to cut out at the bottom: a small pond, a grasshopper and tall grass. The child glues them into the home and draws the frog.

lessons.check: Says three things a frog needs: water, food and a place to hide

titles.picture-tracing-easy-k425-5: Trace and Color the Picture: At the Pond

lessons.title: Frogs and the Pond Tracing: Swan, Ducks and Fish
lessons.objective: Children trace a pond picture, big-middle-small ducks and fish, and pencil paths to turtles and lizards.
lessons.routine: Float paper leaves in the water table and blow them across with straws, then run a finger over the ripples. Lay green paper lily pads on the floor and hop toy frogs across them. Paint long blue wavy water lines at the easel.
week: Water table ripples: blow paper leaves with straws and trace the ripples with a finger.
At the Pond page: trace the swan, the frog, the cattails and the pond, then color.
Blue wavy water at the easel: long wavy strokes across the paper.
Big, Medium, Small page: trace the ducks and the fish from big to small.
Pencil Path Practice: trace lines to the turtles and the lizards.

note.mistake: Children trace the swan's long neck in small jerky pieces and skip the cattails; on the big, middle, small page they trace the fish's outline but miss the fins and the lines on its body.
note.words: Say, "The swan's neck is one long curve. Go slowly." Ask, "Which duck is the biggest? Trace it first." Say, "Don't forget the fins on the fish."
note.watch: At the Pond shows a swan, a frog on a lily pad, cattails, a sun and a cloud; Big, Middle, Small has a row of three ducks and a row of three fish; the pencil path page ends its lines at two turtles and two lizards.

lessons.check: Traces the swan's neck and three ducks in order from big to small

themes.name: Zoo Animals
themes.why: Wild animals at the zoo: lions, elephants, giraffes and pandas, and how a wild animal differs from a farm animal.

titles.picture-word-cards-easy-zoo-animals-k324: Zoo Word Cards: Armadillo, Wolf, Elephant, Lion
titles.picture-word-cards-zoo-animals-k324-195: Zoo Word Cards: Eight Zoo Animals

lessons.title: Zoo Animals Word Cards
lessons.objective: Children name zoo animals (armadillo, wolf, elephant, lion, bat, seal, bear, lemur, koala, giraffe, jaguar, panda) and tell one fact about one of them.
lessons.routine: Build a zoo in the block area with toy animals, block fences and signs with animal pictures. Children are zookeepers: they feed the animals pretend food and tell visitors about each one. Read aloud a picture book about a trip to the zoo. Show photos of a lemur, an armadillo and a jaguar, which are new to most children.
week: Block-area zoo: build fences and put each toy animal in its home.
Zoo Word Cards: armadillo, wolf, elephant and lion; name the armadillo first.
Zookeepers: feed the animals and clap their names: li-on (2), el-e-phant (3), ar-ma-dil-lo (4).
Zoo Word Cards: bat, seal, bear, lemur, koala, giraffe, jaguar and panda.
Zoo guessing game: describe an animal; friends find its card.

note.mistake: Children call the jaguar a "cheetah" or a "tiger," the lemur a "monkey" and the armadillo a "turtle"; they call the koala a "bear" (it is not, but the panda really is a bear). Name the new pictures first.
note.words: Say, "This is a jaguar. Its spots look like little rings." Ask, "Is a koala a bear? It looks like one, but it is not." Say, "A panda really is a bear. An armadillo has a hard shell, like armor."
note.watch: The first page shows an armadillo, a wolf, an elephant and a lion; the second has eight smaller cards: a bat, a seal, a bear, a lemur, a koala, a giraffe, a jaguar and a panda. Watch the names of the new animals.

lessons.check: Names six zoo animals and tells one fact about one

lessons.title: Zoo Animals: Match Them Up, More or Fewer
lessons.objective: Children match zoo animals one to one between two rows and find which row has more, or that they are the same.
lessons.routine: Line up toy zoo animals in two rows and give each animal in the top row a partner from the bottom row. The animals left without partners show which row has more. Then play "feed the zoo": one food block for each animal, and the class says whether there is enough food.
week: Partner animals: two rows of toy animals; give each one a partner.
Feed the zoo: one food block for each animal; is there enough?
More or fewer: count two rows of animals and say which row has more.
Match Them Up page: draw partner lines, circle the row with more, color the star if the same.
Zoo train: give each animal a car; add one car when an animal has none.

note.mistake: Children circle the row that looks longer, even when its animals are just spread out, and draw lines from one animal to two partners; some color the star when the rows only look the same.
note.words: Say, "One line from each animal to one partner." Ask, "Does any animal have no partner? Then that row has more." Say, "If every animal has a partner, color the star."
note.watch: The page has five pairs of rows of small zoo animals (meerkats and big cats, lions and deer, koalas and monkeys, bears and hippos, a zebra and kangaroos); the child draws partner lines, then circles the row with more or colors the star when they are the same.

lessons.check: Matches two rows one to one and says which row has more

lessons.title: Zoo Animals: Farm Animals and Wild Animals
lessons.objective: Children sort animals into farm animals and wild animals and say why zoo animals are wild animals.
lessons.routine: Compare a farm and a zoo: toy farm animals go in a toy barn and toy wild animals in the block zoo. Talk about who takes care of each animal and where wild animals live when they are not in a zoo (jungle, grassland, ocean). Look at photos of lions on the grassland and giraffes eating from tall trees.
week: Barn and zoo: put toy animals in the barn or the zoo and tell why.
Wild homes: photos of lions on the grassland and giraffes eating from trees.
Farm and Wild Animals page: lines from the pig, tiger, horse and giraffe to the boxes.
Zookeeper talk: why do wild animals need so much space?
Wild animal mural with a jungle part, a grassland part and an ocean part.

note.mistake: Children say zoo animals are pets because people feed them, and put the horse with the wild animals because horses run fast; some think a tiger can live on a farm if it is friendly.
note.words: Ask, "Does this animal live on a farm or in the wild?" Say, "Zoo animals are wild animals. Zookeepers take care of them." Ask, "Why can't a tiger live on a farm?"
note.watch: The page shows a pig, a tiger, a horse and a giraffe above a Farm Animals box and a Wild Animals box; the child draws a line from each animal's dot to a box. Listen for "wild" used for zoo animals.

lessons.check: Sorts four animals into farm and wild and says zoo animals are wild

titles.picture-tracing-k418-11: Picture Tracing: A Day at the Zoo

lessons.title: Zoo Animals Tracing: A Day at the Zoo
lessons.objective: Children trace a zoo scene and pencil paths to zoo animals.
lessons.routine: Move like zoo animals: stomp like an elephant, hop like a kangaroo, stand on one leg like a flamingo. Press toy animals' feet into play-dough to make tracks and trace the prints with a finger. Glue craft sticks in a row on paper to build a zoo fence.
week: Animal moves: stomp like an elephant, hop like a kangaroo, balance like a flamingo.
Play-dough tracks: press toy animals' feet and trace the prints.
Pencil Path Practice: trace lines to the monkey, the fox, the camel and the panda.
Craft-stick zoo fence: glue sticks in a row on paper.
A Day at the Zoo page: trace the flamingo, elephant, kangaroo, palm tree and fence.

note.mistake: Children trace the long zoo fence as one line and skip the posts, and they miss the flamingo's thin legs; on the pencil paths they hurry past the bumps to reach the panda.
note.words: Say, "Trace every fence post, up and down." Ask, "How many legs is the flamingo standing on?" Say, "Bump, bump, bump, all the way to the panda."
note.watch: The zoo page shows a flamingo on one leg, an elephant, a kangaroo, a palm tree, a sun, a cloud and a fence; the pencil path page ends its lines at a monkey, a fox, a camel and a panda.

lessons.check: Traces a zoo picture with its fence posts and thin lines

themes.name: Ocean
themes.why: Under the sea: whales, crabs, octopuses and turtles, and how much of our Earth is water.

titles.picture-word-cards-easy-sea-life-bw-2-k3: Ocean Word Cards to Color: Shrimp, Seal, Fish, Dolphin
titles.picture-word-cards-sea-life-bw-k324-169: Ocean Word Cards to Color: Eight Sea Animals

lessons.title: Ocean Word Cards: Sea Animals
lessons.objective: Children name sea animals (shrimp, seal, dolphin, orca, octopus, crab, seahorse, turtle) and tell one way each one moves.
lessons.routine: Turn the water table into an ocean with blue water, sand, big shells and toy sea animals. Children make each animal swim, crawl or float and say how it moves. Read aloud a picture book about sea animals. Show photos of real dolphins, orcas and seahorses, and start a class ocean mural where children add one sea animal each day.
week: Ocean water table: toy sea animals swim, crawl and float; say how each one moves.
Ocean Word Cards to color: shrimp, seal, fish and dolphin.
Ocean mural: add a sea animal and clap its name: crab (1), dol-phin (2), oc-to-pus (3).
Ocean Word Cards to color: pufferfish, orca, turtle, penguin, walrus, seahorse, octopus, crab.
Sea animal parade: walk like a crab, swim like a dolphin, puff up like a pufferfish.

note.mistake: Children call every big sea animal a "shark" or a "fish" (the orca and the dolphin are not fish), call the seal and the walrus both "seal," and think the seahorse is a horse; pufferfish and orca are new words to name first.
note.words: Say, "A dolphin breathes air, like we do. It is not a fish." Ask, "How does a crab walk? Sideways!" Say, "A seahorse is a little fish with a head shaped like a horse."
note.watch: Both pages are black-and-white cards to color: the first has a shrimp, a seal, a fish and a dolphin; the second has eight smaller cards (a pufferfish, an orca, a turtle, a penguin, a walrus, a seahorse, an octopus and a crab). Name the pufferfish and the orca first.

lessons.check: Names six sea animals and how one of them moves

lessons.title: Ocean: Which Sea Animal Is Heavier?
lessons.objective: Children compare two sea animals and decide which is heavier in real life.
lessons.routine: Use a balance scale with beach things: a big shell and a small shell, a cup of wet sand and a cup of dry sand. Children guess first, then watch which side goes down. Then hold a heavy beanbag "whale" in one hand and a light paper "fish" in the other. Talk about real sea animals: a whale is heavier than a school bus.
week: Balance scale: big shell and small shell, wet sand and dry sand; guess, then check.
Hold and tell: a heavy beanbag whale and a light paper fish.
Heavy or Light? page: circle the heavier sea animal in each pair.
How big is a whale? Stretch out a long rope on the playground to show it.
Heavy and light tray: sort the ocean toys into two baskets.

note.mistake: Children pick the sea animal that looks scarier or more colorful, and because the pictures are the same size, the orange starfish and the octopus "look heavy." Real-life size is what counts.
note.words: Ask, "In the real ocean, which is heavier, an orca or an octopus?" Say, "The pictures are the same size, but the real animals are not." Ask, "Could you lift a starfish? Could you lift a shark?"
note.watch: The page shows three pairs of sea animals in equal circles (an octopus and an orca, a shark and a starfish, a whale and a clownfish); the child circles the heavier one in each pair.

lessons.check: Chooses the heavier of two sea animals and explains why

lessons.title: Ocean: Land and Water on the Globe
lessons.objective: Children see on a globe that the earth has land and water and that there is more water than land.
lessons.routine: Toss an inflatable globe ball around the circle: each child catches it and looks where one thumb lands, on land or on water. Make a tally on the chart: water wins. Then build a sand island in a tub of blue water to show land and water side by side.
week: Globe catch: where does a thumb land, on land or water? Mark it on the chart.
Count the marks: there is more water than land.
Land and water tub: build a sand island in blue water.
Land and Water page: color the water blue and the land green (a challenge for the 5s).
Find our country on the class globe and put a star sticker on it.

note.mistake: Children color everything blue, or color the land blue because the ocean is their favorite; many think the white space is snow, and the question "more water or more land?" is hard for 3s.
note.words: Say, "Blue is water. Green is land." Ask, "Is there more blue or more green on our globe?" Say, "We live on land. The oceans are the big blue parts."
note.watch: The page shows a big round earth with land and oceans outlined, a key with a wave (water: blue) and a tree (land: green), a choice between the wave and the tree for "more water or more land," and a star to draw for the United States. Help 3s with the question.

lessons.check: Shows land and water on a globe and says there is more water

titles.picture-tracing-easy-k427-6: Trace and Count: Whales in the Sea

lessons.title: Ocean Tracing: A Turtle and Whales in the Sea
lessons.objective: Children trace a big sea turtle slowly, trace and count whales, and follow pencil paths to sea animals.
lessons.routine: Make waves with a parachute or a long blue sheet, big and small. Draw big circles in wet sand with a finger, like a turtle's shell. Sponge-paint whales at the easel and trace their outlines with a finger once the paint is dry.
week: Parachute waves: make big and little waves with a long blue sheet.
My First Tracing page: trace the big turtle slowly, all the way round.
Wet sand drawing: finger circles and waves in the sand tray.
Whales in the Sea page: trace the five whales, count them and say how many.
Pencil Path Practice: trace lines to the seal, the starfish, the narwhal and the whale.

note.mistake: Children trace the spots on the turtle's shell and skip its outline, or go round the solid frame instead of the dashed turtle; on the whale page they count before tracing and count one whale twice.
note.words: Say, "Start at the dot and go slowly around the turtle, like a turtle walks." Ask, "Did you trace the turtle's head and its feet?" Say, "Trace a whale, then count it."
note.watch: The turtle page has one big dashed turtle with feet, inside a round frame with bubbles (the frame is not traced); the whale page has five dashed whales in the sea, a sailboat, a sun and a box for the number; the pencil path page ends at a seal, a starfish, a narwhal and a whale.

lessons.check: Traces a big shape slowly and counts five traced whales

themes.name: Beach and Summer
themes.why: Summer at the beach: building a sandcastle, beach things, and how the sun warms sand and water.

lessons.title: Beach and Summer: Build a Sandcastle, First to Last
lessons.objective: Children put three pictures of building a sandcastle in order and tell the story with first, next and last.
lessons.routine: Build sandcastles at the sand table or the sandbox with buckets and shovels. Take a photo at each step: smooth sand first, one row of bucket castles next, many castles last. Read aloud a picture book about a day at the beach. Children retell their castle story with the photos and act it out with a bucket and a shovel.
week: Sand table castles: fill a bucket, pat it down and flip it over.
Photo story: take a photo of each step and retell it with first, next and last.
Story Sequencing page: cut the three sandcastle pictures and glue them in order.
Mix-up game: the teacher puts the photos in the wrong order; children fix them.
Tell the sandcastle story to a friend with the glued page.

note.mistake: Children put the picture with the most castles first because it is the "best" one, and the three pictures look alike (the same child at the same beach), so they miss the castles; some glue the strip on without cutting it apart.
note.words: Ask, "What did the beach look like first, before we built?" Say, "Next, there is one row of castles. Last, there are lots of castles." Ask, "How do you know this picture comes first?"
note.watch: The page shows three empty frames on a line (First, Next and Last) and a strip of three small pictures of the same child at the beach: with no sand castles, with one row of little bucket castles, and with many rows. The number of castles is the clue, and it is small: point to it before children cut.

lessons.check: Orders three pictures of building a sandcastle and tells the story

lessons.title: Beach and Summer: Find the Place
lessons.objective: Children count places from the flag in rows of beach things and find first, next and last.
lessons.routine: Line up five beach things on a towel (a bucket, a shovel, a big shell, sunglasses and a water bottle) with a paper flag at one end. Children count places from the flag and play "What is third?" Then line up for the sprinkler or water play, and each child says their place before their turn.
week: Beach towel line: five beach things in a row; count places from the flag.
What moved? Swap two beach things and say their new places.
Sprinkler line: children line up and say their places before their turn.
Ordinal Numbers page: the teacher reads each chip; children count from the flag and mark.
Shell line: set five shells in a row from the flag and find the fourth.

note.mistake: Children count the seagull and the starfish but skip the rock or the bottle because they are plain; others mark the picture that matches the chip's color instead of the picture in that place.
note.words: Say, "Count every picture in the row, even the rock." Ask, "Which beach thing is fifth?" Read, "This chip says third with a circle. Circle the third picture."
note.watch: The page has three rows of five beach pictures (a dolphin, a seagull, a starfish, a swimsuit, a rock, a water bottle, a snorkel mask, a crab, an umbrella, a boat, a sandcastle, a shovel) with a flag at the left and two chips under each row.

lessons.check: Finds the first, third and last thing in a row of five

lessons.title: Beach and Summer: Sun or Shade?
lessons.objective: Children feel things in the sun and in the shade and find out that the sun makes them warmer.
lessons.routine: On a sunny day, set two balls and two buckets of sand outside, one of each in the sun and one in the shade. After an hour, children feel each one and say which is warmer. The teacher touches the slide first, because a slide in the sun can burn, then children feel it and a bench in the shade. Talk about sun safety: hats, shade and drinking water.
week: Sun and shade test: a ball and a bucket of sand in the sun, and another of each in the shade.
Feel and tell: which ball is warmer? Which sand is warmer?
Sun or Shade page: color the circle of the warmer one red and the cooler one blue.
Shade hunt on the playground: find shady spots and feel the ground there.
Sun safety: put on hats, find the shade and drink water.

note.mistake: Children say the shade is "wet" or colder "because it is dark," and color the circle under the picture they like; some think the sun warms things only in summer.
note.words: Ask, "Which ball feels warmer, the one in the sun or the one in the shade?" Say, "The sun warms the ground, the sand and the water." Ask, "Where can we go to cool down?"
note.watch: The page shows a soccer ball in the sun and in the shade, and a bucket of sand in the shade and in the sun, each with a circle; after feeling the real things, the child colors the circle of the warmer one red and the cooler one blue.

lessons.check: Says that things in the sun get warmer than things in the shade

titles.picture-tracing-easy-k431-2: Summer Picture Tracing: Ice Cream Day

lessons.title: Beach and Summer Tracing: Waves and Surf
lessons.objective: Children trace long waves from left to right and summer pictures, and follow pencil paths to beach things.
lessons.routine: Wave a long blue ribbon up and down, slow and fast, then paint long wavy lines at the easel from left to right. Draw waves in wet sand with a stick. Cut a surfboard shape from cardboard (the teacher cuts) and trace its edge with a finger.
week: Ribbon waves: wave a long blue ribbon up and down, slow and fast.
Surf Morning page: trace the long waves left to right, then the surfboard, mask and flipper.
Wet sand waves: draw long wavy lines in the sand with a stick.
Ice Cream Day page: trace the waves, the popsicle, the watermelon and the sunglasses.
Pencil Path Practice: trace lines to the umbrella, the seagull, the beach hut and the hat.

note.mistake: Children trace the long waves from right to left or start in the middle, and the waves go flat on the far side; the popsicle's dots and the watermelon's seeds get traced as scribbles.
note.words: Say, "Waves go from left to right." Ask, "Where do you start? At the left edge." Say, "Little dots on the watermelon: one at a time."
note.watch: Surf Morning has a sun, long wavy lines across the sea, a surfboard, a snorkel mask and a flipper; Ice Cream Day has a sun, waves, a popsicle, a slice of watermelon and sunglasses; the pencil paths end at a beach umbrella, a seagull, a beach hut and a sun hat.

lessons.check: Traces long waves from left to right without lifting

themes.name: Camping
themes.why: Camping outdoors: the tent, the lantern and the campfire, and the sky by day and by night.

lessons.title: Camping Word Cards: Compass, Cooler, Rope, Deer
lessons.objective: Children name camping things (compass, cooler, rope) and an animal campers may see (a deer), and tell how each thing is used.
lessons.routine: Set up a campsite in the room: a sheet over a table for a tent, a cooler, a flashlight, a compass and a short rope kept on a hook to look at. Children pack a backpack for camping and say what each thing is for. Read aloud a picture book about camping by flashlight inside the tent.
week: Classroom campsite: a sheet tent, a cooler, a flashlight and a compass.
Camping Word Cards: compass, cooler, deer and rope; how do campers use them?
Pack the backpack and say why; clap the card words: rope (1), cool-er (2), com-pass (2).
Flashlight story time in the tent with a picture book about camping.
Compass walk: follow the teacher's compass to a hidden "campsite" on the playground.

note.mistake: Children call the compass a "clock" and the cooler a "toolbox" or a "lunch box"; the rope card looks like a broom to many. Some think a deer is a pet you can feed at the campsite.
note.words: Say, "A compass helps campers find their way." Ask, "What do we keep in a cooler? Cold food." Say, "We look at deer from far away. We never feed them."
note.watch: The page shows four big cards: a compass, a cooler, a deer and a rope with a loop at one end and a knot with a frayed tail. Watch for what each thing is used for, not only its name.

lessons.check: Names camping things and tells what a compass and a cooler are for

lessons.title: Camping: Match Them Up, More or the Same
lessons.objective: Children match camping things one to one between two rows and find which row has more, or color the star when they are the same.
lessons.routine: At the classroom campsite, lay out one towel "sleeping bag" for each camper and check whether there are enough: one camper on each towel. Then give each child a flashlight and see who has none. At the camp table, put one cup on each plate and find the extra plates.
week: One for each: one towel sleeping bag for each camper; are there enough?
Flashlight match: one flashlight for each child; who has none?
Camp table: one cup for each plate; find the extra plates.
Match Them Up page: draw partner lines; circle the row with more or color the star.
Pine cone rows: two rows of pine cones; do they match one to one?

note.mistake: Children draw lines to the nearest picture instead of across the rows, so some get two partners; when both rows have four, they still circle one row because they expect something to circle.
note.words: Say, "One line to one partner." Ask, "Does every deer have a partner? Then they are the same, so color the star." Ask, "Which row has some left over?"
note.watch: The page has five pairs of rows of small camping pictures (four deer and four kettles, four grills and three compasses, two raccoons and five backpacks, four kayaks and five lake pictures, five ropes and four life jackets); only the deer and the kettles are the same, so the child colors that star; every other pair has a row with more.

lessons.check: Matches two rows one to one and colors the star when they are the same

lessons.title: Camping: Day and Night Outside
lessons.objective: Children sort things into day and night and talk about what campers see and do when it gets dark.
lessons.routine: In daylight, go outside and list what is in the sky: the sun, clouds, birds. Then make the classroom campsite dark: lights off, a flashlight on the ceiling and paper stars. Children listen for night sounds on a recording (crickets, an owl) and say why campers need a flashlight at night.
week: Day sky outside: list what we see (the sun, clouds, birds).
Night campsite inside: lights off, a flashlight and paper stars; listen for night sounds.
Day and Night page: lines from the bird, the comet, the star and the sun to the boxes.
Flashlight shadows: make hand shadows on the tent wall.
Day and night book: draw one thing campers do in the day and one at night.

note.mistake: Children say the sun "goes to sleep in a tent" and put the bird in the night box; the comet is new, and many call it a rocket or a fire.
note.words: Ask, "When do campers need a flashlight?" Say, "A comet is a ball of ice and dust with a bright tail." Ask, "Are the stars there in the day? Yes, but the sun is too bright to see them."
note.watch: The page shows a bird, a comet, a star and a sun above a Day box and a Night box; the child draws a line from each dot. Name the comet first and listen for reasons that use light and dark.

lessons.check: Sorts the sun, a star and a bird into day and night and explains

titles.picture-tracing-k418-9: Picture Tracing: Camping by the Lake
titles.picture-tracing-easy-k426-2: Where Do I Start? Campsite Steps

lessons.title: Camping Tracing: Tent, Campfire and the Lake
lessons.objective: Children trace a camping scene, follow a step-by-step trace from each dot, and trace pencil paths to camping things.
lessons.routine: Build a pretend campfire from paper towel tubes and orange tissue paper and trace its flames with a finger. Hang a sheet tent over a rope between two chairs (the adult ties it). Trace triangle tents and zigzag mountains in the sand tray.
week: Pretend campfire: tubes and tissue-paper flames; trace the flames with a finger.
Sheet tent and sand-tray triangles: trace tent shapes with a finger.
Camping by the Lake page: trace the tree, the tent, the fox, the campfire and the duck.
Where Do I Start? page: begin at each dot and trace the tent, the tree and the kite down the steps.
Pencil Path Practice: trace lines to the raccoon, the lake, the lantern and the grill.

note.mistake: On the step-by-step page children start anywhere instead of at the dot and lose the arrows; on the campfire they round off the points of the flames, and the tent's triangle is left open at the bottom.
note.words: Say, "Find the dot. That is where your crayon starts." Ask, "Which way does the arrow point?" Say, "Close the tent at the bottom so the rain stays out."
note.watch: Camping by the Lake shows a tree, a tent, a fox, a campfire, a duck, a sun and a cloud; Where Do I Start? has a tent, a tree and a kite down a staircase, each with a starting dot and arrows; the pencil paths end at a raccoon, a lake, a lantern and a grill.

lessons.check: Starts each trace at the dot and closes a triangle tent
